The notion that a 125 GeV Higgs boson perfectly fits the theory of electroweak symmetry breaking can be confirmed, but does require verification of the predicted ratio of Higgs decay modes to bottom and top quarks. Precise determination of this ratio involves measuring the Higgs decay width into a pair of bottom quarks with high accuracy. To this end, our research focuses on the Higgs decay width into a pair of bottom quarks that each subsequently fragment into three jets of charm, up quarks, or light mesons. Utilizing a parton showertime approach, we have derived an expansion of the rate into bottom quark pairs that includes the effects of gluon radiation between the two bottom quarks and their time-like development. Our findings have been compared with existing experimental data and predictions from various Monte Carlo event generators, showing a consistent assessment of the theoretical uncertainty of this decay width. Specifically, we found the theoretical prediction for $ \gamma_{b\bar b} $ to be approximately 0.56 MeV, with a standard deviation of 0.02 MeV. This research is relevant to ongoing and near-future experiments aimed at accurately measuring the Higgs decay width into a pair of bottom quarks.

We have developed an innovative unknoting technique that utilizes minimal crossings to distinguish between knots, incorporating elements from the determinant and intersection-based methods. This approach allows us to create unique, reduced representations of knots and prove that two knots are irreducible variations of each other. Our process can be applied to knotted rings and has been successfully tested on randomly generated links. Notably, we observed that a significant proportion of randomly created links can be easily unknotted using our method.

Given a tropical curve $\mathcal{C}$, previous research established that the set of functions from $\mathcal{C}$ to $\mathbb{R}$ can be expressed as a collection in one-to-one correspondence, using which we define an embedding to obtain the set of functions from $\mathcal{C}$ to $\mathbb{R}$. In this work, we demonstrate that this embedding results in a finite collection when the tropical semifield underlying $\mathcal{C}$ is $\mathbb{R}$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the embedding yields the same collection of functions as the tropicalization of the embedded algebra, with a key proviso that the embedded algebra is expressed in a specific form. A consequence of this research is a finite representation for the set of functions from a tropical curve to any tropical semifield that is isomorphic to $\mathbb{R}$, facilitating a connection to the algebraic-geometric duality.

Given any oriented link L in three-dimensional space, we can establish a unique set of relationships using the intersection points when a certain surface is projected onto the plane. These relationships can be expressed as a system of equations and, when solved, yield specific values for integers associated with the link's properties. When we modify the link by introducing small deformations without disrupting its orientation, these integer values change in a predictable manner according to a defined pattern. This predictable change is reflected in a particular combination of of the values which, interestingly, corresponds to the Euler characteristic of the modified link's surface. Based on this connection, we can define a new mathematical characteristic for oriented links, which we can then use to distinguish between links that cannot be transformed into each other. Furthermore, this new characteristic allows us to demonstrate that a particular set of links contains only one unique member. Additionally, we can apply this new characteristic to a set of links obtained by combining two basic links, the trefoil and the Hopf link, to show that all links within this set can be transformed into each other.

New analysis by the KATRIN collaboration has significantly reduced the likelihood of certain extremely low neutrino masses, lowering the possible range by which neutrino masses could naturally occur. As a result, we have established more stringent minimums for the combined mass of all three neutrino types and the maximum individual mass of a single neutrino type. These new constraints also make it more challenging for some theories that attempt to explain the small size of neutrino masses within the framework of the Standard Model, leading to a more stringent limit on the constant that determines this relation and increasing the predicted value for the number of degrees of freedom in the universe by a very small amount.

Nesta apresentação, exploraremos as técnicas de implementação de uma função de multiplicação de matrizes, que é uma operação fundamental em diversas aplicativas, incluindo redes de rede neural. As abordagens sequenciais e paralelas para o cálculo matricial serão discutidas, com ênfase nas características do sistema de computador que influenciam a escolha da técnica a ser utilizada. Além disso, realizaremos experimentos práticos para comparar o desempenho das duas abordagens em ambientes de software livre.

In an environment threatened by an adversary, multiple cooperative agents must work together to achieve their common goal. The objective involves destroying all enemy agents in a set of locations or preventing an enemy that can move between these locations from remaining. The cooperative agents are situated in the same environment and are able to see each other's positions, yet their movement is restricted to specific areas corresponding to their existing positions. Each cooperative agent has a unique area that it can move into, while the adversary is free to move between all locations. The goal of the cooperative agents is to destroy all enemy agents in the form of an oranges-and-apples type of problem where their attack and defense capabilities overlap. The problem becomes more complex as the number of cooperative agents and areas increases, yet it can be solved with a method that involves collaborative decision-making.

In quantum field theory, perturbative expansions are often inaccurate due to rapid convergence. This issue is addressed by accurately capturing leading logarithmic corrections, which can come from two sources: soft and collinear sectors. Our research focuses on combining leading logarithmic corrections from both sectors to enhance the precision of predictions, with an emphasis on incorporating higher-order effects in the infrared (IR) and ultraviolet (UV) sectors. This involves an expansion in $\alpha_s$ and $\alpha_s/\pi$, with power-law and exponential suppressions, respectively. To achieve this, we need to address two open problems: how to relate soft and hard amplitudes in the IR limit, and how to handle the UV-IR mixing phenomenon. To make progress in this area, we need to consider amplitudes in the large-$N$ limit and explore the properties of IR-finite parts of amplitudes in various $N$-color scenarios. This research also reveals the limitations of the approach, particularly in $s$-channel divergent amplitudes and certain $N$-color scenarios, where additional suppressions arise, posing a significant challenge for this approach.

In this research, we uncover novel attacks that take advantage of the relaxed data controls often found in the context of a federated education setting, particularly in situations where there's a hierarchy involved. By taking a closer look at how a student answers multiple-choice questions influences their teacher's election chances in an election, we reveal an attack that can successfully identify sensitive information about the student by analyzing the teacher's voting behavior following a series of quiz submissions. This attack not only applies to a broad range of subjects but also has the capability to be executed even with a significant number of questions being randomly selected from an larger pool of content. Furthermore, we also demonstrate an additional attack that can pinpoint location-based information about a user by manipulating the voting process in a location-based election within a federated education setting. To counter these types of attacks, we propose an innovative privacy-preserving protocol that combines secret sharing with homomorphic encryption to safeguard against a range of attacks including our newly discovered ones. This protocol is not only effective against the attacks we identified but also provides a secure framework for supporting a broad range of services within a federated education setting.

Kernel-based methods have emerged as a key solution for manifold learning and non-linear dimensionality reduction, but their scalability is limited due to high computational costs and large memory requirements. To overcome these limitations, we propose a new, data-dependent kernel function that leverages the Fourier features of a random linear transformation to achieve both computational efficiency and a reduction in memory usage. The key benefits of our approach are: (i) significant reductions in computational and memory costs, (ii) preservation of the original geometry, and (iii) seamless integration with popular kernel-based algorithms. Our innovative method involves kernel estimation through the use of a random linear transformation in Fourier space, and we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to several real-world datasets and comparing it against other dimensionality reduction techniques.

The primary function of the Cartesian Decomposition method in this work is to demonstrate that certain elements within a specific group can be effectively expressed as a product of elements from another group sharing the same underlying manifold structure. In essence, this involves identifying whether a particular element, originating from the A$_{N-1}$ simple Lie group for a given N, can be reconstructed as a product of elements originating from the B$_{N-1}$ simple Lie group. Building upon this foundation, this research extends its focus to exploring the behavior of these products when the underlying manifold structure undergoes a modification. Ultimately, this leads to the identification of novel embeddings within the B$_{N-1}$ simple Lie group, which can be perceived as mirrored reflections of Garrett's classic embedding for the A$_{N-1}$ simple Lie group.

This research paper investigates how conformal variations affect the Mobius curvature of compact, conformally smooth hypersurfaces embedded in $(n+1)$-dimensional Euclidean space. Building on earlier work by Wang and Wang, we demonstrate that when the Mobius curvature is zero, the same result is obtained under the conditions that the hypersurface has a positive radius of curvature and does not contain lines. Additionally, we establish that a compact, conformally smooth hypersurface with zero Mobius curvature and a positive radius of curvature in $(n+1)$-dimensional Euclidean space is geodesically complete and has a certain inflexibility property.

In congenital heart disease, surgical planning is a complex procedure that requires precise understanding and manipulation of intricate cardiac structures. Although a common approach to this process involves cardiac magnetic resonance imaging-based segmentation, a significant obstacle exists due to the rarity of certain congenital heart conditions, resulting in which there are limited datasets available for training and testing models. This study investigates the potential of a trained U-Net model, using adult cardiac MRI data, to be a reliable tool for segmenting structures in rare congenital heart diseases, for which there is a limited dataset. Evaluating the performance of this model on two-part MR images of left and right heart structures, the results show that it achieves an overall Dice coefficient of 0.857, a mean surface distance of 6.56 mm and a ratio of large to regular outliers of 0.047. Furthermore, user study feedback also indicates that the performance of this model is satisfactory for surgical planning purposes. This study provides evidence that a U-Net model trained on adult cardiac MRI data can be an effective solution for segmenting structures in rare congenital heart diseases, for which there is a limited dataset available, making it a viable option for surgical planning.

This study develops a novel approach to modeling fractures using gradient enhancements for both isotropic and anisotropic materials. The approach enhances the standard brittle model through the introduction of a specific rate-dependent surface differential inclusion, effectively capturing the characteristics of stick-slip behavior. The model's key benefit lies in its ability to model various types of fractures, including those in porous media, according to Kachadse-Pepelea, Grujic, and Aleksic among others, without requiring specific preparation of the surface. Building on the work of Mielke, it utilizes a weakener that attenuates the model's singular forces, enabling existence and uniqueness proof of the solution within the context of a semi-discrete scheme. Ultimately, this approach enables numerical simulation of the anisotropic fracture model.

A new framework for an OFDMA-based multi-user wireless system that combines data and energy transfer is presented. An optimization problem is formulated to balance competing demands for efficient data transfer and reliable energy supply. Resource allocation and power transfer are optimized through an iterative algorithm, ensuring non-empty subchannels and avoiding low-power deliveries. The proposed solution ensures convergence and effectiveness, and is supported by numerical and simulated results demonstrating its efficiency.

Multi-item electronic markets without a central authority face challenges 
in facilitating trustworthy and effective exchanges of trade. Existing research 
on single-item markets extensively leverages mechanisms from the theory of auctions, 
while more recent research on multi-item markets lacks a unified framework and 
often skips examination of individual items in favor of aggregated approaches. We 
propose a novel framework centered on item-by-item assessment and develop a model 
in which multiple items are traded both privately and publicly with varying levels 
of revelation. We examine seven distinct multi-item scenarios and demonstrate 
how different revelation patterns influence desired behavior. Our findings reveal that 
even modest levels of revelation about private valuations can significantly 
improve desired behavior and that fully public knowledge has a more limited impact. 
We also introduce an innovative approach to testing the effectiveness of our 
framework and find results replicable with a separate set of randomly generated 
items. Our research provides a more comprehensive understanding of how to handle 
multi-item exchanges and highlights the importance of considering each item's 
unique characteristics.

Conditional independence models are used in various fields, including statistics, control theory, and computer science, to describe how random variables relate to each other. Given a set of jointly distributed random variables, the conditional independence structure represents the independent relationships between them. The study focuses on extreme cases of such models, specifically those that are minimal and maximal. It has already been established that all models can be achieved through a localized modification of a given model. This research further reveals that any model can be reached by a combination of both localized and global adjustments from another model. It also demonstrates that if a model is indecomposable, all of its components are indecomposable as well. It is interesting to note that not all decomposable models have indecomposable components. It is also shown that the number of possible indecomposable tringles is 52, and they can be distinguished based on their components' second and third level dependencies. It is interesting to note that not all of these tringles can be reached by a combination of two independent tringles.

This paper focuses on solving the term sense disambiguation problem using a
recently introduced method called BERT-based contextualized vocabulary.
Particular attention is given to a model called GlossBERT of Huang et al.
GlossBERT was found to be a strong contextualized model that accurately
predicts the context in which a word appears. Several experiments were
conducted to evaluate the performance of GlossBERT on term sense disambiguation
tasks. It was observed that replacing BERT with GlossBERT for a masked language
model led to a significant improvement in scores. Notably, replacing the contextual
prediction task with a context prediction task for BERT resulted in a greater
improvement. This suggested that the existing strategy of BERT for contextual
prediction contributes to its poor performance on tasks like TSD. Furthermore, a
comparison with the state-of-the-art models on the WordSense Embedding Evaluation
Benchmark revealed that models based on GlossBERT outperformed BERT-based models.
Overall, our research demonstrated the superiority of contextual prediction models
like GlossBERT over masked language models for BERT-like architectures applying
for TSD.

Understanding complex procedures requires not only reading text but also seeing video and interacting with hands-on demonstrations through various interfaces. To grasp these expert skills, we need to consider not only textual descriptions but also visual and auditory cues found in procedural expertise that are presented through multiple modalities. In this research, we first establish a framework for comprehending expert skills that involve multiple modalities by drawing on previous work on low-level cognitive processes and joint attention, and then design an interactive system that can understand expert procedures presented through different modalities. We tested and compared different versions of this system by having human users assess its ability to understand procedures presented through different modalities, and we verified its effectiveness by conducting actual training sessions with users.

In the early stages of a graph theory attack on a network, the graph is modified by removing nodes that have multiple connections, as they are more vulnerable. This paper analyzes the distribution of a specific type of graph that results from this attack, known as the graph of a group G, which is based on the edges generated by the product of any two random group elements. By assuming that any two random group elements are independent and unrelated, the probability of an edge existing between two group elements is 1/2, regardless of the properties of the group. This probability remains the same even when analyzing different types of graphs, such as regular graphs and graphs with varying connection degrees. This paper also explores various methods of graph construction, such as Chordless cycles and Barabasi-Albert graphs, and finds that the distribution of the graph of a group G is closer to a regular graph than other types of graphs. This finding has implications for the security of distributed systems, as it determines how easily a graph attack can spread from node to node.

A fundamental property of the Airy kernel is its universality in one dimension, which has been extensively studied. Building upon this finding, the Airy kernel's universal behavior is demonstrated in higher dimensions for a specific type of polynomial that shares similarities with the Baxter-Zamolodchikov equation. The research establishes that the scaled double scaled Airy polynomials exhibit the same statistical properties as the uniform distribution on the unit interval, thereby extending the principles of one-dimensional universality to higher dimensions. The investigation involves employing the discrete stochastic model, followed by a discrete-to-continuous passage, which yields key insights. The findings also reveal that the associated kernel, which arises from the boundary values, demonstrates the same universal behavior as the one-dimensional kernel. The research further shows that the same universality properties are exhibited by the scaled tridiagonal matrix ensemble in a specific regime. The findings are verified through numerical simulations, which demonstrate excellent agreement with the predicted universal behavior. The research provides a clear explanation of the conditions required for the universality to be observed, which involves the matrix having a specific non-trivial invariant subspace. The study demonstrates that the scaled tridiagonal matrix ensemble shares a close resemblance to the Gaussian orthogonal ensemble in a specific regime, which involves the ratio of its dimensions tending to a specific value. The research offers a novel perspective on the underlying structures that are necessary for the universality to be observed.

To optimize the performance of advanced gravitational wave detectors, next-generation sensors are being developed for seismic protection and vibration monitoring within these sensitive facilities. Research has led to the creation of the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer, a novel technology that outperforms conventional sensing methods by minimizing optical distortion and increasing data accuracy. Characterized by low noise at high frequencies and excellent linearity, this new sensor has been thoroughly tested, showing its effectiveness and reliability. In practical applications within sensitive gravitational wave detectors, such as LIGO 3G, the sloshing-Sagnac sensor has consistently met expected performance standards.

Recent research has investigated the complex interplay between non-overlapping field-of-views and transmission patterns in multi-input and multi-output wireless communications. A new study develops an accessible protocol called XL-MIMO ASP, characterized by a flexible transmission angle that can be adjusted freely. The research then proves that a key performance indicator, the non-overlapping coverage probability, is optimized when the transmission angle is twice as wide as the field-of-view. Furthermore, the analysis demonstrates that increasing the number of antennas does not significantly impact performance and offers a practical solution for antenna array sizing. The study's findings are theoretically justified by proving that a key performance indicator can be optimized even without considering non-overlapping visibility areas in certain scenarios.

Recent observations at sub-millimeter/millimeter wavelengths have revealed that many young stellar objects are surrounded by irregular or fragmented substructures in their protoplanetary disks. To better understand the origin of such findings, we investigate the vertical structures formed when protoplanetary disks with non-axisymmetric density variations undergo the vertical shear instability, using numerical simulations that incorporate the effects of gas-grain chemistry and turbulence on disk properties. Our analysis reveals the presence of molecular species that can bind to dust grains, contributing to their growth, and demonstrates how this process is affected by the conversion of gravitational energy into heat and the instability's amplitude. As the annealing of volatile species on grains occurs, water and organic molecules vaporize, forming volatile dust complexes, often fragmented, and sometimes resembling ring-like patterns. These species binding to dust grains facilitate their growth through shear instability, and this process is fueled by the conversion of gravitational energy into heat, as well as the instability's amplitude. Our research also shows that organic molecules can bind to dust grains in a similar manner to water, and both can contribute to the growth of dust complexes through the vertical shear instability. These findings have implications for the development of planetary systems, as they may lead to the formation of chondritic asteroids and influence the early development of planetary systems through gravitational scattering and other planetary system architecture formation processes.

The concept of "big apple strength" is introduced to describe a hypothetical composite system of highest stability, comprising three fundamental components: protons, neutrons, and a central force that maintains equilibrium. By adopting this idea, the characteristics of central forces that contribute to strong interactions among protons and neutrons can be deduced through a reverse engineering approach. These central forces are identical to those proposed by the "solitaire bag model," which are fundamental in understanding the internal structure of finite nuclei, as well as infinite matter and rotating, stratified astronomical objects like neutron stars.

As part of a broader effort to address electronic complexity, we've developed an efficient framework for solving strongly correlated models using first-principles methods. Our approach combines the efficiency of density functional theory with the capabilities of dynamical mean-field theory to capture local interactions and lattice effects. To streamline the process, we've introduced a strategy for using approximate models that incorporate detailed band structures without requiring the use of tight-binding approximations. Our method allows us for an accurate representation of the local hybridizations in models like the one for SrMnO$_3$, enabling a more precise capture of the local physics and reducing the need for the adjustment of parameters. By applying this method to SrMnO$_3$, we found that the local magnetism in this material is robust, but we also found that a more precise representation of the band structure is necessary in order to capture the phenomenon of electron transfer between the $p$ and $d$ orbitals.

This research focuses on creating superposition-based quantum gates, specifically the Molmer-Sorensen gate, using trapped ions coupled with a thermal gas of motional modes. A critical requirement for these gates is that the motion of all trapped ions be cooled to near-lower-temperature equilibrium. Our study finds that, even if the trapped ions' motion is balanced but not perfectly synchronized with an internal clock, the proposed Molmer-Sorensen gate remains frequency-resilient (less than 2 percent error). We demonstrate this capability experimentally using two- and three-body entanglements and show that even with a range of frequency deviations exceeding the beam frequency, the desired outcome can be achieved. This finding provides a foundation for securely performing quantum operations on trapped ions even in environments with significant thermal vibrations.

Using advanced computational models, we investigated the random arrangements of atoms in paraelectric perovskites, commonly used in piezoelectric materials like barium titanate. By applying thermodynamic integration and using structures modeled by molecular dynamics, our studies revealed the average, paired arrangements of atoms that are essential for maintaining the paraelectric state. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that local order exists even in the absence of long-range order, potentially providing a more fundamental explanation for the phenomenon of ferroelectricity. By considering entropic effects and defining a specialized interaction strength, our results may also be applied to study other phase transitions in materials with complex structures.

We examine a series of layered compounds based on MnBi, which recently showed isolating the Dirac electrons within a single layer of the crystal structure, in detail. Our research particularly delves into the unusual properties of MnBi$_5$O$_{10}$(OH)$_2$ and MnBi$_2$O$_4$, in which the Dirac electrons are linked to the layers' strong interlocking. We developed a model that accurately represents these interconnections and accurately accounts for the band structure formation. Our analysis indicates that the interconnections significantly impact the isolated Dirac electrons' behavior, modifying their mobility and overall isolation. As a result, we predict that these compounds will exhibit unique, high-carrier-mobility isolated Dirac phases.

This research introduces a framework that addresses three fundamental questions related to the interaction of multiple frequency or ratio values within a single dimension. The proposed framework is applicable to various statistical measures, including means, medians, and ratios. It is particularly useful in analyzing data that is bimodal, containing two distinct groups with different frequency or ratio patterns. The framework consists of four conditions that must be met: (1) the distribution within each group is stable; (2) the groups are distinct and not merged; (3) the data is bimodal; and a fourth condition that is yet to be defined. This study demonstrates how the framework can be employed to examine the distribution of data within each group by partitioning the data and conducting within-group comparisons. It also facilitates an exploration of the data's bimodal nature. The framework is an advancement over previous work, notably the work of Baggs and Allison (2009), and is illustrated using an example based on their study.

The NA62 experiment at CERN can provide significant evidence for the existence of a neutral leptons of abnormally low mass by thoroughly examining the $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$ process. To accomplish this, the experiment must thoroughly examine the existing limitations of other searches and reinforce current restrictions on a specific neutral lepton generation that could be responsible for various anomalies observed in $K$ decays. In order to establish these constraints, the experiment must thoroughly examine the $K^+ \to \pi^0 \nu X$ process in addition to its primary goal of discovering neutral lepton generation. As a result, the experiment will be able to establish the most stringent constraints to date on a particular neutral lepton generation that could be responsible for several anomalies observed in $K$ decays by thoroughly examining the $K^+ \to \pi^0 \nu X$ process in addition to its primary goal of discovering neutral lepton generation.

In a Sagnac interferometer, typically used for detecting tiny variations, a unique phenomenon called a spectral shift anomaly occurs. This anomaly is linked to the curvature of light within a specific framework, known as the Galilean frame. The spectral shift anomaly can be understood through the principles of light's curvature and the effects of relative motion within this particular framework. The laws of physics remain consistent across all frameworks, implying that the spectral shift anomaly observed in a Sagnac interferometer is an inherent property and is not dependent on the specific framework in use.

This work extends and refines the findings of choice of smooth point for parabolic triples in the context of flag varieties and reductive groups, specifically within Type A. The focus is on determining the nilpotent fibre's structure through the Weierstrass form of the adjoint representation, particularly for parabolas. The approach developed employs geometric methods, utilizing Poincare duality and Lefschetz fixed point theorem to achieve this goal. The study reveals the structure of the nilpotent fibre for non-degenerate and degenerate parabolas alike, encompassing situations where the Lie algebra's highest root is embedded within the parabolas' direction. The research also delves into examining components of the nilpotent fibre of minimal Levi subalgebras, primarily the solvable part sharing a long root with the Lie algebra, and provides a description of its structure.

Neural language models have seen significant advancements in recent years, yet they require vast amounts of training data and typically overlook the power of $n$-gram models. We propose a unique approach that combines the strengths of both models by using a residual learning framework. In this method, a neural language model is tasked with refining the predictions made by an initial $n$-gram model for masked words. Our approach simplifies the neural model's training process by reducing the necessary training data and minimizing the computational resources needed. When testing our approach on the GLUE tasks, our results indicate that it yields superior performance compared to a single neural model, and surprisingly, the residual learning method even outperforms $n$-gram models on the LMLM baselines. In addition, our method exhibits impressive efficiency and a notable reduction in the required training data.

We provide a detailed explanation for our recent findings related to three-dimensional $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano triroids in a companion paper. This explanation serves as a preliminary to our main theorem proving the association between certain type of complete three-dimensional $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano triroids and one-dimensional $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano del Pezzo surfaces via the Laurent transformation.

Reconstructing and aligning faces in images is a challenging task, primarily due to the vast range of variations in lighting, expression, and pose. This paper introduces a groundbreaking innovative method, SADRNet, to create a three-dimensional representation of faces through a novel self-aligned dual facial regression framework. This framework leverages two unique components: a pose-alignment module and a reconstruction module that are integrated to deliver exceptional performance. The pose-alignment module and reconstruction module are interconnected yet independent, allowing them to be trained and optimized individually for maximum effectiveness. The team behind SADRNet has made the model available for public use and has achieved notable success, as evidenced by their results.

Locally invariant quantum field theories have traditionally been the primary focus of study. This work deviates from this norm by proposing a class of theories whose symmetries are only observed in a lattice-like structure, derived from the spontaneous breakdown of translation invariance. Our analysis indicates that such theories' low-energy characteristics are determined by modes that lack momentum dependence and are bound by discrete amounts. This minimality constraint leads to an unusual constraint on the low-energy theories' dimensions and their interaction strengths. Our study reveals that the modes responsible for this behavior are 'fractons,' a term we use to describe quasiparticles with discrete momentum movements. These findings are demonstrated through an efficient description of lattice theories based on Weyl fermions both in two and three spatial dimensions. In these cases, we show that the efficient field theories conform to the general principles we established in advance. Our analysis also facilitates the evaluation of lattice theories' low-energy properties in a more efficient manner.

In the early stages of the universe, a slow-roll inflation period likely occurred, shaping the cosmos as we know it today. Despite this, the universe's initial conditions, which led to the emergence of structure and the formation of black holes in the distant future, remain unclear. This study delves into the relationship between slow-roll inflation's disturbances and the formation of primordial black holes, focusing on the $k$-inflation model featuring a $\alpha$-attractor potential. By examining the power spectrum of cosmological perturbations and the primordial power spectrum, this research aims to identify potential constraints and underlying parameters that could lead to PBH creation, offering a pathway for better understanding the universe's early future through the analysis of future gravitational wave observations and potential constraints on the primordial power spectrum.

Researchers examining the structures of ordered trees have identified a significant point - a vertex that is not a leaf node - and have assigned it the label 'deepest' if there is no child node further down the tree's depth. This notion has been applied to a specific type of ordered tree known as a labeled ordered tree. A previous study established the probability of an edge node being the deepest vertex in a labeled ordered tree of n vertices. This paper will expand on that finding by calculating the probability of a non-edge vertex being the deepest vertex and deriving a general formula for the distribution of the deepest vertex in a labeled ordered tree. A key insight was that the distribution of the deepest vertex is independent of the tree's shape and is instead determined by the number of children each vertex has. This is in contrast to other properties such as the distribution of the highest or middle vertex. This independent relationship was used to derive a closed-form expression for the expected value of a function of the deepest vertex. This result has implications and could be applied to other problems involving the expected value of a function of a non-leaf vertex. A related open problem is mentioned at the end of this paper.

The accuracy of election outcomes relies heavily on manual and machine-based methods of counting ballot votes, where each step is susceptible to human error. The process of optical character recognition in elections involves multiple stages, where a single misstep can compromise the validity of the results. Existing OCR systems are effective but often lack the ability to verify their findings, which is crucial in the close margins often seen in election outcomes. To address these concerns, we present an informed OCR system that not only accurately identifies characters but also checks the ballot's integrity and verifies voter participation. In our approach, we utilize a unique combination of neural networks to validate the ballot's format and voter input. We tested our system against existing methods and found it to have a significantly lower error rate, which we have openly shared for further comparison and validation.

In recent years, the success of large-scale linear models has sparked great interest. Research into their fundamental properties has yielded significant insights, particularly in models trained on independent and identically distributed data. However, the behavior of linear models in time series settings remains less understood. This paper explores the properties of over-determined linear models in time series contexts, focusing on how the model's parameters evolve over time. A key finding is that over-determined linear models exhibit an 'benign misfitting' property, where their parameters are influenced by past observations in a manner that becomes increasingly diffuse over time. This research has implications for the development of linear models, enabling them to effectively utilize all available historical data when estimating parameters. A practical approach, incorporating a student-t distribution to model the long-term memory of past observations, is also presented. This approach is shown to be computationally efficient and outperforms traditional methods in simulation scenarios and real-world applications.

Effective noise reduction in speech improvement remains unaddressed. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel deep learning attention bidirectional model that enhances single-channel speech quality. The proposed model leverages an intricate attention mechanism, allowing residual learning to focus on critical frequency components and irrelevant noise periods. Moreover, it employs a complex bidirectional structure to combine forward and reverse RNN information, ensuring a comprehensive understanding of speech segments. Experimental results on the CHAIN and ICBRI corpora demonstrate that our attention bidirectional model excels over existing methods, yielding superior MSED values of 6.54 dB and 8.95 dB respectively, along with improved segmental SNR values of 13.16 and 16.67.

The rise of digital influence and social media has created unprecedented opportunities for the rapid dissemination of malicious content, including cyber threats. To explore this phenomenon, we introduce the concept of "information pathogens" - harmful online entities that spread through digital "seeds" and thrive in the interconnections of modern online connectivity. To study the dynamics of information pathogens, we examine the spread of online music videos on YouTube and the implications for audiovisual content, revealing how features like emotional resonance can amplify a pathogen's impact and reshape online culture in the process. By distilling the principles of cyber influence into a set of "laws of the digital age," our research offers insights for both online content creators and security specialists seeking to navigate the complex landscape of online connectivity.

The growing complexity of distributed modern electricity systems demands a more sophisticated analysis of electricity storage's functional capabilities to ensure a stable and secure grid operation. Besides their primary function of balancing supply and demand, storage systems can participate in stabilizing the grid through various services like frequency regulation and contingency response. While storage's potential in distributed markets has been identified, there's a lack of research on incorporating its functional capabilities in planning and operation. Current storage planning approaches focus solely on its balancing capabilities, ignoring its potential in grid services. This paper introduces an innovative method for self-planning storage by considering its functional capabilities, enabling storage systems to participate in both balancing and grid stabilization services. A case study in a large distribution network reveals that considering storage's capabilities in self-planning can increase the number of controllable megawatts in the network by 15 times, while a storage unit's estimated costs are $141, respectively, for balancing and grid stabilization services.

In complex systems, superfast electron processes often occur, but their significance is frequently lost due to insufficient temporal resolution in standard spectroscopic techniques.  For a binary transition metal oxide, CuO, we employ femtosecond laser-based diagnostics to investigate matter and electron dynamics. A novel technique was developed to determine the rapid decomposition of Auger electrons under intense near-infrared fields, and a unique phase space for these electrons was mapped. The results indicate that in an intense IR field, the energy of the electrons is increased by a minimum of 2U (where U represents the Auger energy) to at least 3U, and that this energy can be achieved through a process of triply resonant two-electron transitions. The duration of this interaction was found to be in the range of several hundred femtoseconds to one picosecond, and the dependence of the electron dynamics varies based on the initial state of the system. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that the proposed diagnostic technique can be employed to investigate other electron processes that are relevant across multiple fields of science and application.

As planetary systems are discovered at an increasing rate, astronomers are able to observe diverse configurations of planetary systems around stars and this variety is reflected in a higher number of notable exoplanets found so far, particularly those of significant size that could potentially support life. Research on these potential life-hosting worlds is focused not just on their formation but also on their atmospheric conditions and whether they can support life through various methods, such as temperature maintenance or existence of biomolecules in the atmosphere. Studying atmospheric processes in these exoplanetes involves using global circulation models that are also employed to analyze atmospheres in gas giants around stars of different temperatures. Although general circulation models are highly detailed, they are also highly expensive to operate on current computational resources, especially when modeling time periods as short as several days for highly rotating planets that are expected to be in a state of continuous cyclonic rotation. In contrast, simplified models like the one introduced in this paper are more cost-effective as they still capture the fundamental circulation patterns in planets that are highly rotating and have large distances between atmospheric jet streams. By applying these models to multiple planets ranging from slowly rotating ones like Mars to highly rotating ones like UPSILON-1b and comparing their results, this paper presents the atmospheric circulation patterns in these planets. In the first part, the results for the three planets UPSILON-1b, KELT-9b and HAT-P-65b are presented. UPSILON-1b, the most rapidly rotating planet

Research has shown that learning from a single data source can be optimized by controlling the magnitude of the model's parameters during training. This study delves into controlling another critical factor: the model's output magnitude when training on ImageNet. By investigating the effects of controlling output magnitudes in addition to parameter magnitudes, the study reveals that dynamic learning based on both criteria can yield superior performance. Specifically, the study finds that incorporating an L2 penalty for the sum of the squares of the output magnitudes when training yields a 0.6% improvement in top-1 accuracy. Moreover, dynamic learning according to this dual criterion is found to allow for a 3 times reduction in batch size while maintaining the same level of performance, thereby implying substantial cost savings in distributed training settings.

In 1851, Hermite introduced the algebraic frequency as a parameter in the theory of equations. Over time, researchers have been motivated to classify polynomials based on properties derived from this frequency. Our work classified polynomials by geometric properties and introduced new parameters, such as the geometric frequency of a complex polynomial, which is closely linked to its algebraic counterpart. We established a bimodal classification that connects both frequencies and proposes a method for constructing polynomials with specific algebraic frequencies. Our approach also enables the creation of complex polynomials from given parameters, including the geometric frequency, which determines the shape of the polynomial's roots in the complex plane.

We examine the interaction between a type of rare earth atom, specifically dysprosium, and a cavity field for purposes of developing an all-optical method of creating and controlling the motion of a single atom. We find that a specific combination of light frequencies can generate an exact imitation of the motion of a charged particle in a one-dimensional harmonic potential using the atom-cavity system. By applying this phenomenon through electromagnetic induction in a surrounding vacuum, we observe similar motion in a nearby superconducting resonator even when the atom is distant from it. We utilize this relationship to devise a method for controlling the motion of a superconducting resonator that is spatially separated from the dysprosium atom. Notably, we discover that when we have two specific frequencies of light interacting with the dysprosium, it results in a complex potential of the one-dimensional harmonic type, a phenomenon not seen with a single atom. This leads to the generation of a squeezed state in the superconducting resonator, allowing it to serve as a source of a specific type of light state. We also find that when we have two dysprosium atoms, it gives us the ability to measure the optical phase by detecting a specific state in the superconducting resonator, a function that cannot be performed with a single atom.

To accurately model donor atoms embedded in silicon, researchers use the effective mass theory, simulating donor behavior through a simulated "effective weight". By combining the simulated effective weight with careful consideration of valley and spin interactions, they derive a comprehensive simulation framework. This study takes a novel approach by employing a complex simulation framework that considers the unique properties of silicon's electron valleys and the intricate spin interactions. In contrast, traditional models employ a simpler "single effective weight" approach. The research involves a collaboration between theoretical and experimental silicon researcher groups. It provides a detailed explanation of how to employ the "many effective weights" approach, specifically utilizing a specific "donor-pair" setup. The study also offers a framework for other silicon donor simulations. Furthermore, it highlights the significance of precise simulations for future silicon-based quantum computing applications.

Our investigation reveals that a HgTe layer lacking a bandgap can function as a quantum channel for the observation of chiral phenomena. We have designed a HgTe/GaAs superlattice with "trench"-like structures, consisting of thin, non-inverted bandgap HgTe regions surrounded by wider inverted bandgap HMer layers. We have determined that the HgTe regions experience significant strain-induced spin splitting, sufficient to bridge the bandgap, yet only in the 'trench' areas due to their smaller size. As a result, we create a quasi-two-dimensional system where the band edges meet, enabling efficient, asymmetric carrier transport. A notable feature of this system is the existence of a quasi-Dirac cone near the edge of the heavy hole band. We have established that a substantial, external longitudinal magnetic field can convert this quasi-Dirac cone into a true Dirac cone, leading to massless, relativistic carrier behavior. We have developed a comprehensive theoretical framework to analyze the electronic and transport properties of this unique system and have validated our model using an 8-meV resolution mid-infrared spectroscopy, demonstrating that our model accurately predicts carrier behavior. This research examines a crucial aspect of 5G technology, specifically its ability to handle road safety applications in areas with high traffic interference. Focused on a section where roads intersect, we investigate how an adaptive Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access (NCMA) system impacts data transfer between vehicles. Initially, we develop mathematical models representing the relationship between NCMA's parameters and its performance, leveraging Moment Generating Function (MGF) methods. We then investigate two scenarios to analyze performance: first, by evaluating NCMA's effectiveness when there's significant interference between vehicles, and second, by assessing its impact when the interference is minimal. Key findings include: employing NCMA can enhance data transfer transfer rates, with a 20% increase in rate when interference is substantial and a 10% boost when interference is mild; moreover, adjusting NCMA's parameters to match the level of interference can yield up to a 30% improvement in transfer rate; finally, in scenarios with mild interference, using a conventional Orthogonal Multiple Access (OMA) system may also yield comparable results to NCMA. These discoveries have implications for the implementation of 5G technology in transportation systems and highlight the need for further research aimed at fully harnessing the technology's potential.

In a 5G system, Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD) enables efficient spectrum utilization by allocating flexible time slots for uplink and downlink transmission. However, TDD's performance can be affected by strong uplink transmissions, which can cause downlink receive interference. We have developed a stochastic model to capture this interference and other factors affecting TDD allocation, and we employ non-cooperative game theory to derive efficient allocation solutions. By formulating a submodular function based on our model, we obtain an approximate solution with a 1/e factor of optimal value when users make independent decisions. We also analyze the impact of cross-slot interference and mobile edge computing on 5G TDD allocation. Numerical simulations validate our approach and demonstrate its performance in real-world scenarios.

This research investigates Hall irreversibility in a fixed lattice of vortices through vortex-core disorders. A quantitative examination of the irreversibility line in a BSCCO thin film reveals that the volume fraction of vortices exhibiting Hall irreversibility is substantial, estimated to be around 10%. Notably, the temperature at which the irreversibility is minimum is found to be very close to the normal-to-parallel transition temperature within the vortex state. The findings suggest that normal-to-parallel transitions within the vortex state play a crucial role in determining Hall irreversibility.

The fixed point properties of second-order cumulants in the 3D Ising universality class have been examined using the functional renormalization group in both the high-temperature phase and at the critical temperature. The investigations were conducted for a variety of models, including the 3D Ising model itself, and found to be in alignment with the expectations derived from the renormalization group. A notable discrepancy was found in the comparison of the fourth cumulant to the square of the second cumulant in the high-temperature phase. The analysis indicates that the ratio exhibits temperature dependence, in contrast to the predicted universal behavior. The universality of the 3D Ising class is also explored through a comparison with the mean-field model, which serves as an example of the tricritical universality class. The results show that the ratio of the second to the first cumulant exhibits temperature-dependent behavior, in contrast to the predicted universal behavior. The ratio of the fourth cumulant to the square of the second cumulant displays a greater discrepancy with the predictions of the renormalization group, particularly in the critical region. The ratio exhibits a more pronounced difference in the critical region in the comparison with the mean-field model. The issue of the temperature-dependent behavior of the fourth cumulant is addressed in the conclusion section.

Given any finite-dimensional vector space, denoted as $V$, over the field of complex numbers and any non-negative integer $n$ representing the depth, we can define a specific type of operator algebra known as the bimodule inclusion series, symbolized as $\boxtimes_{i=1}^n M_{k_i}( \mathbb{C} )$. This operator algebra forms a subfactor that's self-duplicate under repeated application of the standard invariant, known as the Haagerup approximation, and eventually reaches the base case of $\mathbb{C}$ after $n$ iterations. By analyzing the structure of the commutant of $\boxtimes_{i=1}^n M_{k_i}( \mathbb{C} )$ and applying the Haagerup approximation, we can derive a description of the corresponding subfactor for any given $n$. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the approximation and a specific pattern, known as the fusion ring, and explore its implications. By examining the relationship between the ring's additive and multiplicative structures, we can identify a pattern that predicts the existence of a particular sequence, even if it can't be directly derived from the available data. This prediction is validated for all values of $n$ up to $4$, and it reveals a connection between the subfactor generated by the square of a particular algebra and its relationship to the representation of a symmetry group known as the A3 category, which is closely linked to

In this work, we examine the potential of using Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HamNNs) to obtain gradients for optimizing the performance of a target model, a capability commonly referred to as'reverse mode of operation'. We contend that HamNNs can indeed be trained to generate high-quality gradients at a significantly lower computational cost compared to the usual method using backpropagation through time (BPTT). To achieve this, we formulate the optimization of HamNNs as an objective function that can be solved by integrating the desired performance metric with respect to the model's parameters, a problem whose solution is well-defined up to an arbitrary constant. We further propose a practical integration strategy that leverages a hybrid approach combining analytical and numerical integration methods. We provide empirical evidence of HamNN's ability to produce accurate gradients and its computational efficiency by conducting comprehensive experiments across multiple model architectures, dataset platforms, and performance metrics. Notably, we observed a 2-5 times speedup in training time compared to BPTT.

The success of an AI system depends heavily on its reliability component, yet surprisingly, there is a lack of research that addresses this aspect. Focusing on enhancing the reliability of AI through a collaborative human-artificial system approach, we developed a framework that integrates multiple agents working together and with humans in an iterative process. This framework incorporates a reliability agent that utilizes machine learning models and gathers trust ratings from humans to determine data quality and take corrective actions to prevent the degradation of data and models. We tested this framework in a simulated environment and found that it yields significant improvements in model performance and reliability. Additionally, we applied this framework to a real-world scenario involving a classification model for detecting malicious traffic and achieved a notable increase in accuracy and a substantial reduction in model failures.

In recent years, X-ray-based security scanning has gained significant attention as a reliable method for detecting prohibited items. Although deep learning techniques have improved detection accuracy, there's still a notable gap between performance on real-world images and artificially created datasets used in benchmarks. To bridge this gap, researchers introduced a high-quality dataset consisting of real X-ray images for security examination, alongside a novel context module that aims to prevent the detection of banned items. This module and the newly created dataset are intended to enhance the efficacy of X-ray-based security scanning by improving the ability to identify prohibited items in real-world images.

We introduce a newly developed superquantity, denoted as $Q_V$, which is based on a specific type of mutation called the Lefthermius mutation. This superquantity is utilized in conjunction with a modified version of the Mumford's system to create an invariant for torus bundles with a volume hypothesis. Moreover, we demonstrate that this invariant has the capability to distinguish between distinct torus bundles. Furthermore, we establish that our construction is a representation of the quantum invariant developed by Morita and Sasakura for torus bundles with a volume hypothesis. Additionally, we provide an explicit formula for our construction and an intuitive explanation of the volume hypothesis in terms of this formula. We also provide an illustration of how our construction can be employed to identify distinct torus bundles.

The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning have led to improved performance in WSD tasks, nonetheless several elements hinder progress in this field including a lack of contextual information in classification models and the limited availability of annotated data.  Contextual embeddings like BERT deliver a context that encompasses word order and other essential details, nonetheless they are expensive to use in a large-scale WSD setting due to the extensive nature of the embeddings.  In order to address these challenges a novel framework known as the Context-gloss Enhanced (CEN) model is proposed that incorporates a novel approach to supplement contextual embeddings with additional context that is used for enhanced semantic information.  Several context-gloss creation strategies are proposed and employ a combination of part-of-speech tagging along with a neural coreference model to generate a gloss that is used as an additional feature for a multi-view learning based WSD classifier.  The proposed CEN model framework is evaluated on three datasets and the results demonstrate its superior performance when compared to the conventional context-gloss baseline models.

The reciprocal gamma function is often represented through its integral definition in one dimension, and our study explores the application of regularized techniques to transform it into a well-defined and finite integral. We successfully demonstrate the use of several methods, including the cancellation of divergent terms, logarithmic transformation, and change of variables, to obtain a finite and regularized form of the one-dimensional reciprocal gamma function. Furthermore, we derive the proposed regularized form and show that it is compatible with the original function, and we investigate the one-dimensional regularized form in higher dimensions.

In proton-nucleus interactions, identifying the top quark relies on detecting at least three charged particles with high momentum or one charged particle with high momentum and significant missing transverse momentum. The standard method used in proton-proton interactions is ineffective due to a higher background rate in proton-nucleus interactions. A new method has been developed to increase the detection probability of the top quark by a factor of five hundred, even in events where the decay products do not have enough momentum to enter the detector's acceptance range. This method involves searching for events with a high momentum imbalance and a substructure within one of the jets, which significantly enhances the detection of the W boson and top quark. Furthermore, if the nucleus has sufficient mass number, the position of the proton's entrance within the detector can be used to enhance the detection probability by another factor of ten.

The task of text-to-SQL parsing allows a system to generate accurate SQL queries directly from natural language input, but current approaches are hindered by the limited scope of training data available. To tackle this limitation, we propose expanding the training data to include unrelated text samples that are not connected to any specific database. In our approach, we separate the text-to-SQL parsing task into two distinct challenges: first, understanding the intended meaning of the text, and second, translating that understanding into a valid SQL query. We then propose a new task that combines these two steps, where two separate inputs are transformed into a single unified SQL query output. To accomplish this, we develop a multi-task framework that utilizes two separate encoder-decoder models, and also explore various ways to interconnect these models through additional auxiliary tasks. Our results demonstrate notable improvements over existing baselines on the SuperGLUE dataset, achieving a significant boost of 20.8% in accuracy.

Machine learning models reliant on data have evolved significantly, with a growing dependence on structured data found in graphs. These models now tackle complex challenges like image recognition, natural language processing, and predictive analytics. Despite their numerous benefits, they also raise confidentiality concerns, as a breach of differential privacy could occur when training on sensitive graph data without proper safeguards. Researchers have developed various techniques to protect graph data from unauthorized access and sensitive information leaks, safeguarding against attacks that exploit training processes. This survey explores techniques like noise addition, encryption, secure multi-party computation, and private machine learning, as well as attacks like information leak, overfitting, and utility loss. It also delves into private training methods, including federated learning, model watermarking, and obfuscation, and highlights the need for private inference, real-world case studies, and a summary of open issues in the field.

As the largest digital archive of paintings ever created, the collection from the Paris Louvre will significantly benefit from advanced technologies used in the thorough examination and detailed study of artworks. Euclid's innovative methods of aging star observations will, in fact, introduce a novel approach to assess the environmental conditions affecting the paintings in the Louvre's exhibition halls. This project will not only contribute to the advancement of heritage science but also offer opportunities for training, given the complex nature of data analysis.

In evaluating autonomous driving systems, a key consideration is their ability to handle complex road networks, which are not easily created using traditional methods. Current techniques used in the industry are time-consuming and labor-intensive, requiring significant human effort and involving real-world safety risks when implemented in actual vehicles. To address these limitations, we propose an automated method for generating challenging road networks that are tailored to evaluate the system's ability to navigate complex situations. By leveraging Bezier curves and a randomized search algorithm, we create a flexible and efficient system for producing high-quality test scenarios that are both aesthetically pleasing and realistic. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we include an application example that utilizes our system in conjunction with the Gazebo simulator and the OpenCV library.

Melody captioning is introduced as a groundbreaking task that goes beyond existing music retrieval approaches. To lay the groundwork for future research in this area, a comprehensive dataset called HSingMelodies is developed to facilitate training and system assessment. This dataset is a collection of text descriptions accompanying a diverse array of popular Chinese songs. In addition, a novel evaluation framework is presented to thoroughly examine the performance of melody prediction models. To achieve this, both direct and indirect assessment methods are employed, leveraging multiple metrics including BLEU, ROUGE, CIDEr, meteor, and mean average precision. Through extensive experimentation with various deep learning models, improvements in performance have been observed, and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of the evaluation framework. Furthermore, key findings indicate that there is a clear disparity between the perceived artistic value of music and its objective technical aspects.

Quantum Bose fluids, whether from supercooling atomic gases or lattice systems, exhibit complex behavior under both steady-state and non-equilibrium conditions due to their interacting nature. Even though hydrodynamic models have been successful in capturing some key features, there is a significant need to incorporate the quantum properties that are fundamental to these systems. A new quantum hydrodynamic model has been developed that accounts for the interplay between interactions and random thermal fluctuations and is applicable for both coherent and turbulent regimes. This model demonstrates its utility by accurately predicting several prominent features, including a non-zero chemical shift in equilibrium and the onset of a sudden transition from a coherent to a chaotic state in non-equilibrium conditions. Furthermore, it provides a framework for investigating any steady-state or quasi-steady situations, as well as a method for obtaining initial conditions for any given non-equilibrium situation, making it a valuable resource for the study of these fluids.

Temporal activity detection, the task of identifying recurring events within a continuous time series, is a crucial aspect of monitoring seismic activity. Although machine learning methods have demonstrated superiority over traditional approaches, they suffer from a significant drawback - the requirement for labeled data to train models. A novel technique, called the dual context aggregation network (DCAN), has been developed to detect seismic activity without the need for labeled data. Seismic events exhibit consistent patterns, which DCAN models as a inherent property. It achieves this by designing a dual-context framework that aggregates information from two context windows - one containing recent data and the other encompassing more distant information. In turn, this enables the model to focus on the time frame directly affected by the event. In a comparative study with six different models, including a standard classifier and unsupervised methods like one-class SVM and elliptical boundary model, DCAN demonstrated superior performance in detecting seismic activity.

The paper delves into the origin and defining characteristic of "Palm Tree Modes" - a specific edge edge-localized mode in tokamaks. It distinguishes Palm Tree Modes from other ELMs through a unique symmetrical magnetic field component and sharp, rapid changes in edge current density. Research indicates these modes propagate at nearly the speed of light, with significant impacts on plasma and divertor components, and are linked to low-density edges and sharp temperature gradients, though the exact cause remains unclear. No consensus has been reached regarding a theoretical model that accurately explains these modes.

This research focuses on preventing collisions among autonomous mobile robots moving autonomously within a static environment, where visual information is used for navigation. As a mobile robot navigates, it creates a vortex potential region around itself that changes over time and is shared with other robots through a local communication network. This region serves as an indicator of the robot's intended path and is utilized by neighboring robots to take avoidance measures. The proposed method ensures that collisions are averted by ensuring the vortex potential region of one robot does not intersect with the designated safety area of another robot. This is achieved through the collaborative robots adjusting their paths to maintain a safe distance from one another. An efficient algorithm is presented, and its performance is validated through simulated and actual trials showing that the approach effectively prevents collisions in various scenarios.

In the context of the Ewens sampling model representing a random partition of integers according to their prime factorization, we determine the limiting behavior of the normalized sum of independent random variables, where the normalization scheme deviates substantially from the standard method used in the central limit theorem. This involves dividing the sum by a multiple of the minimum rather than the maximum of the standard deviation and the square root of the sample size. We find that under certain conditions, the resulting distribution converges to a specific asymptotic form, and this convergence occurs at a rate influenced by the Euler phi function. This development extends to a broader class of models that incorporate additional parameters, exhibiting more intricate structures.

Recent advancements in wireless communications have been influenced by the concept of metasurfaces, particularly passive reflectors like intelligent surface systems (IRSs). To explore the potential of these systems, we will examine how a simple radar system can benefit from an IRS located in the target's line of sight. By integrating the IRS, we discover that the radar system experiences enhanced performance, including improved accuracy in estimating target speed, orientation, and shape, as well as increased effectiveness in distinguishing between multiple targets. To achieve this, we develop a novel method for estimating the relative distance and shape of a single target and a method for differentiating between multiple targets by analyzing changes in the reflected signal's polarization characteristics. This research offers a foundation for exploring more complex scenarios, such as active communication systems and self-contained IRS systems.

Achieving optimal coverage in an application through testing is often determined by various factors including taint analysis, data flow, and pattern-based methods. However, there is no universally accepted standard to evaluate and compare fuzzers, testing methodologies commonly employing these techniques, as the effectiveness of a fuzzer significantly relies on the method of evaluating it. Given that different evaluation methods can yield distinct outcomes, it becomes necessary to standardize a common framework for comparing and testing the versatility of fuzzers across diverse applications. This paper presents a range of advanced evaluation methods, including both automated and manual approaches, tailored to assess the coverage of a fuzzer, and makes the test cases and evaluation methods it presents available to the research community.

Significant advancements have been achieved in models that learn from raw text, particularly in tasks where knowledge is applied after a period of time has passed. Despite the progress made in testing these models on individual tasks under their own conditions, there is a lack of comprehensive evaluation. The existing assessments tend to focus either on simple tests or complex real-world applications, missing the middle ground entirely. In order to address this gap, we introduce the Basic Benchmark, which requires models to learn basic mathematical facts from a relatively small amount of text over time. The benchmark exhibits challenging characteristics for testing the effectiveness of pretrained models in a learning scenario, including: understanding basic language to compensate for limited instructional text; grasping abstract concepts behind the text, such as sequences and patterns; and evaluating understanding through both direct and indirect assessments. The benchmark also offers adjustable variables to explore multiple aspects of ongoing learning, such as the rate of new information intake and the duration of time elapsed since initial exposure. Through our research on the Basic Benchmark, we discovered that the performance of pretrained models can be quite poor, often failing to break 50% accuracy just a day after initial exposure. This finding highlights the need for further exploration into how to enhance the performance of models on tasks that involve the application of previously learned knowledge over time.

This research paper focuses on minimizing surfaces within a specific metric area in three-dimensional space and identifies them based on a given homotopy type. Although the term "surface" is not strictly defined by a boundary in three-dimensional space, it can be defined in a way that allows the comparison of different surfaces belonging to the same homotopy type through the use of a variation of the isoperimetric problem. This study establishes that surfaces minimizing the metric area in three-dimensional space are unique and stable for each homotopy type, including non-trivial types like the one represented by a trefoil knot.

This final installment builds on previous research concerning the extended-time behavior of solutions to semilinear parabolic equations on the real line. Previous findings established the convergence of solutions to a stable equilibrium and the convergence of their derivatives to a limit that may be either finite or infinite, depending on the starting point. This article investigates what happens when the derivative does not converge to a finite limit, revealing that it is impossible without the equation being unstable at some point infinitely far from zero. A key technique employed involves modifying the original equation to create new equations whose solutions' behavior can be more easily analyzed, allowing for the application of a variation of the lemma from Part II.

Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus using the full effective interaction monopole-tensor interaction two-body interaction are presented. This interaction demonstrates high success in describing observed features of the 64Ni nucleus, specifically its low-lying excited states and spin properties. Notably, a unique phenomenon where two-body interactions result in a mix of 0+ and 2+ spin states at the same energy level is observed for the first time. This occurrence, referred to as "form coexistence," provides valuable insight into the 64Ni nucleus and offers a chance to explore null-spin states in a stable nucleus in detail.

The concept of an equilibrium being informationally efficient can be explored through whether sufficient information is available to facilitate the implementation of a suitable strategy. This study focuses on a specific category of games, namely Lipschitz games, characterized by their smooth and non-degenerate nature. The primary objective is to establish an ultimate information requirement for determining an equilibrium that is reachable via an appropriate strategy. The main contribution involves establishing specific lower bounds for the required information, taking into account both the number of actions and the number of players. A notable outcome of this research is the introduction of a direct comparison to the recent findings of Srivastava and Tardos (2019) on the complexity of approximating Nash equilibria. This comparison reveals that the new results provide a more precise upper bound in certain scenarios. A key method employed in this study involves an innovative approach to equating the complexity of an equilibrium to a specific geometric problem. This approach enables a direct link between the information requirement and several existing metrics of complexity, including the notion of strong free public equilibria introduced by Aumann et al. (1995) and the complexity of approximating Nash equilibria. A novel application of this connection results in a related inequality involving the information requirement and a specific product of action-related parameters. This inequality may be of independent interest.

When comparing systems using metrics such as BLEU or ROUGE, a standard practice is to conduct k-fold cross-validation to ensure the randomness of sentence reordering. However, the choice of k is often arbitrarily set to 1, which we argue results in inconsistent results due to over-reliance on a single split. In support of this claim, we observed that results vary significantly with different random splits, leading to a substantial standard deviation when k is set to 1. To address this issue, we investigated alternative settings for k, including those that are a power of two (2, 4, 8) and found that these settings yield more stable results with lower standard deviation. Notably, lower k values generally achieved higher system scores with smaller variance, suggesting that there may be an optimal k that balances system performance and variance. To further explore this notion, we proposed a new validation strategy that dynamically adjusts k based on the observed variance, and found that it yields system performance that surpasses traditional k-fold cross-validation methods. Through our experiments on three prominent NLP datasets, we demonstrated that validation strategies with adjusted k can produce high-performance models with minimal variance.

Recent advancements in imitation learning and teaching methods have sparked interest in structured approaches to how pupils are taught and how they learn.
