In this research, we explore the application of these techniques to enhance the efficiency of false news identification models. By condensing articles before feeding them into the model, we observe a notable improvement in both accuracy and efficiency. Furthermore, our findings suggest that certain automatic summarization parameters such as summary length and metric choice may also be optimized to further boost model performance.

This research investigates how changes in the positive parameter $\epsilon$ affect the behavior of a specific family of Gaussian stochastic fields as it varies across different geometric spaces with changing Ricci and sectional Ricci curvatures. Our study examines the relationship between $\epsilon$ and the long-term memory of the fields, their mixing property, and the conditions required for them to have a stationary mean. Additionally, we provide a comparison of the rates at which the fields' mean and their components converge to the mean converge to zero. Our findings indicate that the behavior of the fields is highly dependent on whether the curvature parameter $\epsilon$ is less than, equal to, greater than, or alternates between 2 and 0. Notably, the fields exhibit distinct characteristics, some of which are analogous to those displayed by the traditional L\'evy-driven stochastic geometric integral fields.

In a secure non-orthogonal multiple access (SEC-NOMA) system, an untrusted user's intentions must be deduced through transmitted signals from a trusted base station. This study focuses on a scenario where a single untrusted user exists and the base station communicates with this user using SEC-NOMA. The primary objective is to develop a method for accurately identifying SEC-NOMA messages to the user by analyzing received signals from the base station. This involves solving a non-convex optimization problem to determine message decoding instructions for the base station. An efficient solution to this problem is proposed, and the effectiveness of this approach is validated through simulation-based analysis.

When dealing with outliers in multivariate data, the use of the $\ell_1$-norm instead of the squared Euclidean distance in dimensionality reduction yields better results. However, minimizing the $\ell_1$-norm of the within-cluster variance for one-dimensional projections proves to be an NP-hard problem. This research introduces an innovative two-step algorithm to extract a one-dimensional feature along a rotation symmetry, first approximating the optimal projection by interpolating rotated versions and subsequently converging to the result using an inexact Newton method tailored to handle the $\ell_1$-norm objective. This new method is compared to the state-of-the-art method by Li et al. through numerical experiments and is particularly found to be more efficient and less sensitive to initial conditions. This research is also extended to a two-dimensional feature extraction application.

The rise of BERT-based models has led to enhanced performance in various natural language processing tasks, including semantic role labeling. These models can be applied to create empathetic dialogue systems by identifying the underlying emotions in user questions. However, improving the accuracy of such models requires human evaluation and model fine-tuning based on correctly labeled data. In this study, we propose an interactive method that combines human intelligence with the learning capabilities of BERT. We develop a platform that allows users to interact with the model through a user interface and adjusts the model's parameters accordingly. Our results show that this approach yields a 19.4% improvement in F1 score compared to the baseline BERT model. The system's ability to learn from human feedback also results in a 34.1% increase in the model's accuracy on unlabeled test data. The code for this project is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/Chenxiao-1994/BERT-SE.

The primary focus of this research is on exploring power series and Laurent series within the context of group rings, specifically those associated with the rational numbers and their relationship to the real numbers in a one-to-one correspondence that's order-preserving. The study establishes that for a specific class of groups, the ring in question admits both power series and Laurent series, before delving into an in-depth analysis of its algebraic properties. The investigation ultimately reveals that the ring is an integral domain powered by a free commutative group, whose elements correspond to non-negative rational numbers.

The X-ray binaries known as polars possess a unique characteristic: their white dwarf spin period significantly differs from the binary's orbital period. This distinct feature, present in a small percentage of non-synchronous polars, is less common than the asynchronous variety. Asynchronous polars have spin periods longer than those expected, given the binary's orbital period, often displaying a correlation with the duration of the system. Both asynchronous and non-synchronous polars exhibit harder X-ray spectra than the general population of low-mass X-ray binaries. However, a notable disparity exists in their X-ray properties: the former tend to display greater hardness when the white dwarf's spin period approaches its synchronization value with the binary's orbital period. This phenomenon is less pronounced in non-synchronous polars. A notable exception is the non-synchronous polar in the binary with the shortest orbital period, which exhibits softer X-ray spectra compared to its counterparts. This exception may indicate that non-synchronous polars with very short orbital periods behave differently due to the white dwarf experiencing magnetic flux dissipation as a result of the binary's close proximity, thus not following the same pattern as the asynchronous polars.

This study aims to illustrate the integrated Reduced Basis Method's potential in solving complex Interactions between a fluid and a deformable structure. We subsequently investigate the benefits and limitations of applying a one-dimensional representation to split the fluid and structure into distinct components, while utilizing a reduced order model for an interconnected weak Form. This research is a response to the growing need for more efficient computational methods resulting from the increasing intricacy of Computational Fluid Dynamics and Structural Mechanics problems.

Building on the concept of topological maps, HiTMap integrates metric information with place labels to assist navigation in unfamiliar areas. HiTMap differentiates between core and peripheral locations within an environment, defining core places as those easily accessible by a person with average mobility, and peripheral places as areas further apart that may require longer paths to reach. The system generates optimal routes between these locations by considering both topological and metric information, prioritizing the most accessible paths between core and peripheral places. HiTMap's unique structure enables a person with limited knowledge of the environment to decide on the most convenient next location to visit, even if it's a peripheral place, by evaluating the topological and distance-based convenience of each location.

The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 SemEval OffensEval Task, which aimed to identify and categorize hateful, offensive, and sarcasm content in tweets, employed a multi-step approach combining BERT and support vector machines. In the initial phase, BERT was utilized to generate various BERT-based features for each sentence, which were then extracted from the tweets. These features were subsequently fed into an ensemble of support vector machines to determine the presence of offensive language and, for cases indicating offense, the underlying category was further refined through additional analysis. The results of our system for the task at hand yielded precise offensive language detection rates and relatively accurate categorization, with space for future improvement and expansion into additional languages.

By utilizing an exact atomic interferometry setup on a atomic beam crossing through a point, we have demonstrated the sensitivity of detecting magnetic field fluctuations at $\Delta B \approx 3.5\times10^{-8}G$ when the atoms are in the center of an atomic interferometry setup, and this increases to $\Delta B \approx 2.5\times10^{-8}G$ when the atoms are positioned at the edges. This improvement originates from the unique magnetic field cancellation in an atomic interferometry setup, which allows us to enhance the sensitivity by approximately 57%. Furthermore, our findings are applicable to various types of atomic beams and suggest the possibility of enhancing sensitivity in related applications such as atomic optical hyperfine transitions.

We have analyzed the unique electronic and magnetic characteristics of two-dimensional materials from the TMDC family and found that some of these materials exhibit intrinsic magnetic properties. We investigated three distinct scenarios in which these materials could be spun: free electrons, electron-hole interaction, and proximity to a metal layer. We discovered that spinning certain TMDC materials can lead to significant changes in their thermal properties, including a change in heat capacity and a phenomenon called the spin-dependent magnetocaloric effect. This effect is particularly notable when we consider that it can be triggered by applying a small amount of pressure or changing the applied electric field, which could provide a non-invasive way to control the magnetic properties of these materials. Notably, this effect can also be achieved over long distances, making it possible to control magnetic properties in materials that are not directly connected to the source of the spin. This finding could open up new possibilities for using TMDC materials in devices that require precise control over magnetic properties.

In a semiconductor quantum well, particularly when it contains a superlattice or an electron gas with strong correlations, the behavior of light is significantly influenced by electrons in a way that breaks fundamental symmetry rules. This influence is mainly electronic when the quantum size is small, and it can be described by a suitable extension of the Pekar parameter, which accounts for the nonlocal interaction between light and electrons. This extended model also considers the movement of electrons out of their initial confined area when light interacts with them. A previous study on this model focused on a quantum well with a relatively large width and found that it resulted in the creation of two photon energy gaps. Contrary to these findings, our research on a quantum well with a very small width shows that the nonlocal electronic effects and the movement of electrons out of their confined area have opposite influences on the creation of photon energy gaps, and that they can either enhance or diminish gaps, respectively. A detailed analysis of these influences is presented when the movement of electrons due to light can be ignored.

Type theory relies on the normalization of terms to derive proofs of validity and ensure the soundness of developments. However, the inherent complexity of the calculus of constructions (CC) renders the normalization task impractical, if not impossible, to accomplish manually, given the sheer quantity of terms existing within its expressive type system. In contrast, an alternative approach, normalization via elimination structures, proves feasible for most types in CC, yet encounters a significant hindrance with the delta operator. This obstruction necessitates the introduction of a new normalization approach, based on a modification of the CC known as the 'extended cc', to overcome the challenge. By normalizing the extended cc, we can confidently assert the proofs of development correctness. In support of this assertion, an implementation of the new normalization approach has been successfully put into practice with the CoC2CoC compiler.

A fundamental model has played a significant role in the development of topological quantum systems: the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. This brief survey provides an in-depth exploration of the SSH model's underlying principles, highlighting its central characteristics and how they impact both atomic and collective phenomena. A diverse range of situations can be represented by the SSH model, including situations with both equal and unequal on-site energy levels, as well as diverse lattice spacing variations. As a result, this review delves into the fundamental aspects of topological quantum systems through the lens of the SSH model, making it relevant to a broad audience interested in physics.

This paper explores the underlying connection between mixture models and the integration of probability measures through the use of Choquet theory. By establishing this link, we demonstrate that both the traditional mixture models and modern variants can be perceived as specialized forms of integrated probabilities. This unified framework allows us to introduce new methods for estimating mixture models, including an approach based on the integration of geometric measures that outperforms existing techniques. Notably, our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in multiple benchmark tasks, especially for sparse and overlapping clusters.

We derive a two-loop amplitude formula for supergravity in AdS$_5$ times S$^5$ using an extension of the impact parameter method, originally developed for flat space gravities. The formula is expressed as the sum of two components: one representing the gravitational and Yang-Mills interactions in flat space, and a third component accounting for the effects of the curved AdS$_5$ space. The formula is found to be in line with the double-copy principle, and a notable feature is the appearance of a duality between two different representations of the AdS$_5$ geometry, mediated by Yang-Mills and a specific component of supergravity in flat space. The formula is tested against existing data, and a notable match is found for a particular subset of amplitudes at this two-loop order. A simpler formula is obtained for a specific subdiagram, and this leads to an observation on the behavior of certain coefficients in supergravity at this order. A connection is also made with a recent observation on the limitations of a particular subset of the bootstrap equations. A more detailed understanding is also gained on the role of color-kinematics, and a specific relationship between supergravity, Yang-Mills, and gravity in flat space, all encapsulated in a reformulation of the double-copy principle.

The current object-based programming models for GPUs lack a suitable memory management system that is both efficient and secure. To overcome this limitation, we present DynaSOAr, a novel concurrent memory allocator designed for object-based programming on GPUs. Built with performance, safety, and ease of use in mind, DynaSOAr allows programmers to manage memory using objects, eliminating the risk of pointer errors and memory leaks. At its core, DynaSOAr features a dynamic pool allocation strategy that minimizes memory fragmentation, waste, and reallocation overhead. It achieves this through the use of a unique "size arithmetic" that anticipates future memory requirements and adapts the memory layout accordingly. Furthermore, DynaSOAr includes a non-blooming tree data structure that facilitates efficient searching and insertion of objects, reducing memory access latency. When put to the test, DynaSOAr demonstrated superior performance compared to traditional host-based memory allocators and a custom GPU memory allocator, showcasing its potential to become a standard memory management system for GPU applications.

This article investigates the boundedness of a diverse set of operators, including those generated by the Calderón-Zygmund operators and the fractional integral operator, when acting on functions within a broader context of mixed spaces known as the generalized mixed Morrey spaces. Additionally, the article examines the boundedness of a specific operator, the Riezs potential operator, is examined on the same type of spaces. Furthermore, the article delves into the study of the commutators created by the interaction of a sublinear operator and a function belonging to the Morrey space, and proves their boundedness on the generalized mixed Morrey spaces.

A new theoretical approach is presented that enables a precise description of the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states an impurity atom or dimer undergoes when situated near the edge of a superconducting gap. This approach is subsequently applied to the examination of manganese adatoms and dimers on the Nb(110) surface to determine the localized Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states and the associated spin-polarized phenomena. A notable aspect of this research is an unanticipated spin configuration on the Nb(110) surface that is in conflict with earlier assumptions and needs to be reevaluated in the study of magnetic and superconducting hybrid materials.

Our proposal, FourierMask, introduces a novel approach to instance segmentation using the Fourier transform to analyze frequency-based component separation in implicit neural representations. FourierMask analyzes the frequency-based properties of the Fourier transforms of implicit function representations and leverages this analysis to improve instance segmentation. In particular, FourierMask evaluates the frequency spectra of the Fourier transforms of the predictions made by an implicit mask representation network and adjusts its parameters to minimize the discrepancy. By doing so, FourierMask succeeds in instance segmentation experiments on the MIST-1M dataset, demonstrating that processing the frequency spectra of the Fourier transforms of predictions can enhance instance segmentation performance.

This research builds on a previous study by Bérard and Gauthier, which utilized the Rauch-Type estimate to demonstrate that a compact, minimally immersed surface in a convex domain within Euclidean space $E^n$ has a perimeter greater than $\pi$ when $n>3$, and a perimeter greater than $2\pi$ when $n=3$. Our investigation extends this finding to a significant degree. By removing the requirement that the ambient space be convex, we demonstrate that any closed, minimally immersed surface in a convex domain within $E^n$ has a perimeter greater than $k\pi$ for $n>3$, and a perimeter greater than $l\pi$ for $n=3$, where both $k$ and $l$ are non-negative constants that can be arbitrarily close to 1.

The formation of a distinct feature - a veiled core - is likely to occur in highly convective cloud formations due to the impact of particle collisions, causing light scattering that results in a darker central area. This study aims to locate this feature in a specific type of cloud using a particular approach to analyze images from space. The approach involves a detailed examination of a particular spectral range, specifically the red edge where the relationship between cloud opacity and imaging data becomes most distinct. By refining the approach to account only for the red edge, the approach uses a method to eliminate the primary factors that affect this spectral range, thereby isolating the contribution of the veiled core. The approach is applied to a selection of cloud formations imaged from space using a particular technique, and the results show that the veiled core can be identified in a significant proportion of the cloud formations examined. The study also finds that the core becomes more noticeable as the cloud becomes less opaque, and a particular relationship between the core's characteristics and the cloud's properties. The study has implications for the use of cloud imaging from space in a particular context, and suggests that a particular approach to analyzing images from space can be a powerful tool.

A new phenomenon occurs in ion propellants, specifically those using a thin, electrically charged layer (the space charge sheath) to propel ions, where a high power electromagnetic wave (the "chirp wave") causes the space charge to become essentially empty, resulting in a significant increase in propulsive efficiency. This improvement arises because the space charge sheath, normally a major source of energy loss due to its interactions with the wave, is temporarily eliminated during this time, allowing the propellant to efficiently utilize the energy from the wave. Several factors contribute to this increased performance: the space charge electric field, which hinders ion acceleration, is greatly reduced; the formation of electron holes, which can impede ion motion, is avoided; and the occurrence of two-wave interactions, which can decrease efficiency, is prevented. A model has been developed to model this environment and several parameters have been identified that affect the two-wave interaction and the resulting space-time electric field. Notably, this environment allows for the efficient use of a wide range of frequency ratios between the wave and the ion propellant, a key advantage over traditional ion propellant designs. Monte Carlo simulations have also validated the findings of the model.

In this research, 13 new planets were discovered among 7 exoplanet candidates from previous findings, with four notable discoveries standing out. TOI-712 b and c, two close-orbiting mini-Neptunes, were found with a 2.5-day circular rotation pattern. TOI-712 d, a larger and more distantly rotating world, was discovered in an 11.4-day circular orbit. TOI-712 E, a low-mass world with a 4.3-day circular rotation pattern, was found to be the innermost planet of the system. In addition, two potential planets, TOI-712 F and G, were identified but in need of confirmation. Furthermore, this study provides an accurate assessment of the system's mass and how the planets formed and evolved within it. Models indicate that the planets formed through the cooling of a disk system and the gravitational interactions with two massive early-formed cores. The study also sheds light on how the inner planets were affected by the system's migration, with potential for future research on the system's formation and evolution.

This investigation employed density functional theory to examine how carbon and nitrogen impurities affect the electronic and magnetic properties of rutile titanium dioxide. Although previous studies found these elements generally lower the energy required for excitation in TiO$_2$, this research delves deeper by analyzing the specific arrangements of impurities and their impact on both localizing magnetic moments and band gaps. Computational simulations indicate that substituting nitrogen for oxygen produce stable defect states that could facilitate dye-sensitized photocatalytic reactions under sunlight. In contrast, carbon-infused locations are less favorable due to increased energy needed for excitation, and potential magnetism only occurs with unique, double-doped configurations.

Although the precise measurement of top-quark production has been extensively confirmed through various searches, our research focuses on an underexplored aspect - the elastic creation of top-quark pairs in proton-proton collisions at the LHC. We propose an innovative method to identify this process by analyzing the behavior of protons scattering off each other at very small angles, where we can determine the missing momentum carried away by the neutrinos. By incorporating advanced neutrino reconstruction techniques and optimizing existing detectors' capabilities, we aim to detect this rare phenomenon through excesses in proton-proton elastic scattering at very small angles. Our approach involves integrating data from different proton-proton collision energy settings, where we can find the top-quark pair production signature at an expected rate of approximately 24 femtobarns of integrated luminosity. This research is supported by theoretical models predicting a non-negligible fraction of top-quark pairs created elastically, which could be as high as 10^-8 in the case of production at an elliptical polarisation of -0.1. If proven, this could provide a unique framework for testing the standard model of particle physics.

The precise observation of stellar oscillations in the intra-cluster atmosphere of M17 has been used to determine the level of turbulence in a study that aims to establish a relationship between the turbulence and mass loss in massive star-forming regions. By applying a new method for determining structure functions, the study assesses various sources of error, including instrumental limitations, the effects of stellar activity, and the presence of stellar oscillations. The study finds that the most significant constraint is posed by the instrumental limitation, which significantly exceeds the expected value of turbulence before considering the effects of stellar oscillations. The study suggests that future observations utilizing radio systems with greater sensitivity and resolution could potentially recover more accurate information about turbulence in regions like M17.

In 1993, Erdos and Galvin solved Ramsey's high density triangle problem by a mere 3 days over requiring a polynomial bound. Building upon their work, we obtain a more substantial advancement where we establish the Ramsey number for a specific dense subgraph within an infinite graph, specifically for a subgraph equivalent to a triangle, although the specific triangle configuration is infinite rather than the standard three-connected one. Specifically, given any two infinite graphs F and G that satisfy a certain condition (an edge in F connects two vertices v and u if there exists another vertex x in G such that the connection between v and x, and between u and x, respectively, corresponds to a triangle), we aim to find the minimum proportion p of edges within an infinite graph G that guarantees any subgraph with density p contains a copy of F. Our result holds under the assumption that the Ramsey number in question is greater than a certain arbitrarily set number.

Located in the heart of the Milky Way lies the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), a ring-shaped region where molecular gas and star formation are concentrated. To better understand the mass distribution within the CMZ, we employed a two-dimensional correlation method to analyze 1.3 mm continuum sub-petasescond Submillimeter Array observations. By identifying sub-petasecond dust emission in the CMZ, we were able to measure the mass arrangement down to a few parsecs in scale. The mass distribution analysis indicates that the CMZ has a non-axisymmetric mass arrangement, with mass density increasing by a factor of more than ten in the molecular ring's inner region compared to the outer areas. Furthermore, mass density shows a notable enhancement of a factor of over five in the Sagittarius A* (SAA) complex in relation to the surrounding areas.

Identifying Bell's Palsy through video analysis has the potential to provide rapid, cost-effective, and non-invasive diagnosis. Our research focuses on a unique approach, leveraging eye movement analysis on short video segments. We conducted two independent studies to evaluate this method's effectiveness. First, we examined 19 subjects with confirmed Bell's Palsy and gathered 83 eye-centered data sets from 4-second video clips. Our model's accuracy in detecting Bell's Palsy in these subjects was 55.4%. To ensure the method's validity and minimize potential biases, we collected additional data from 19 individuals without Bell's Palsy, gathering 83 eye-centered data sets. Unfortunately, our model failed to distinguish between subjects with and without Bell's Palsy in this expanded dataset. As a result, we were unable to achieve a higher overall detection rate. Furthermore, we observed significant challenges in differentiating Bell's Palsy patients with normal eye movements from those with abnormal eye movements associated with the condition.

The quantum electrodynamics in su(1,1) de Sitter space, known as sQED, is a renowned theoretical model that has been extensively studied in both classical and semi-classical forms. Researchers have recently simulated sQED using quantum systems in both one-dimensional lattice configurations and through the application of quantum circuit architecture. These simulations have exposed various phenomena, including the creation of stable, low-energy photons and interactions that are not present in regular QED. However, the availability of higher-energy photons is limited in these simulations, constraining our access to a comprehensive understanding of sQED. In this study, we build upon previous work involving the quantum circuit quantum electrodynamics model by incorporating depth-agnostic sound enhancements to our quantum simulator, allowing us to efficiently obtain higher-energy photons. We demonstrate that introducing a controlled interaction between the qutrit and sound wave mode can effectively split a low-energy qutrit state into two non-overlapping states at higher energies. We also establish the accuracy of this method by calibrating the energy transfer using both theoretical modeling and experimental measurements. Furthermore, we find that the energy of the qutrit can be increased by a factor of up to 40 over its coupling with the photon field. We anticipate that this advancement will significantly enhance the simulation of sQED, enabling the exploration of qutrits in multiple degrees of freedom that are fundamental to this theory.

The proposed future Electron-Ion Collider will allow for in-depth research of the spin structure of nuclei using highly polarized, high-energy electrons. Achieving this level of polarization in the electron beam requires a significant amount of radiation, specifically from a thin, intensely irradiated solid-state target illuminated by a high-power laser. The process is as follows: the interaction between the laser and the target creates an intense stream of polarized positrons, which are then reversed in polarity and directed back at the target where they can interact with the ions. If the positron polarization can be maintained until they reach the detector, this process could provide the necessary polarization for the electron beam. However, due to various factors such as radiation effects and positron accumulation, ensuring sufficient polarization requires thorough understanding and modeling of the positron production and polarization dynamics. This paper presents a comprehensive simulation of positron generation, including their polarization properties, based on the interaction of laser and electrodynamically accelerated and thick carbon foil targets. The model accounts for the effects of a potentially thick target on positron polarization, which could result in significant reduction due to the increase in scattering and other interactions that can alter the polarization of outgoing positrons.

This research paper examines a novel concept called a limited group, which is essentially an abelian group based on the unique combination of its elements. In essence, two generators are enough to reconstruct the entire group. We've developed two primary results: Firstly, we prove that any finite limited group can be represented as a direct sum of isomorphic cyclic groups. Secondly, we demonstrate that an infinite limited group contains a finite limited subgroup with the largest possible size, and this size is equal to the number of elements in the infinite group. This result does not extend to non-abelian groups, as an infinite simple group like the one discovered by Burnside contains an element with a specific combination that cannot be expressed using any combination of the other elements.

A miniature temperature detector has been designed, featuring high accuracy and a compact footprint. Capable of operating across a broad voltage range from 0.6V to 1.8V, the design leverages a bistable switching mechanism to calculate temperature, employing a sub-threshold voltage of 0.15V $\pm$ 0.05V for maximum precision. The temperature indicator comprises a complex digital display, enabling easy reading of temperature values. To minimize power consumption, the unit incorporates an innovative power-saving circuit that switches between operating and standby modes based on temperature levels. During normal operation, the detector consumes 20.01 $\mu$A, while the standby circuit draws 0.55 $\mu$A. The device exhibits minimal error, with a difference of up to 1.4°C from the actual temperature and a high degree of precision, reaching as low as 0.24°C. Transformed into a CMOS process, the design demonstrates exceptional resilience and minimal variation, achieving a high degree of reliability.

Long-lived stars experience significant internal dynamics that can cause their internal structure to change over time, affecting the stability of their magnetic fields. This study investigates how non-uniform, adiabatic perturbations of long-lived stars' magnetic fields are stabilized by their internal dynamics, specifically the interaction between convection and the perturbed magnetic field. By analyzing the growth or decay of perturbations, this study determines the relevant time scales and establishes the conditions under which a star's magnetic field can be stable. Key factors influencing stability include the non-uniformity of the perturbation and the star's convective properties. This research builds on previous findings related to the stability of stars' magnetic fields in [1] and provides a more comprehensive framework for assessing stability that accounts for both radial and non-radial perturbations.

In this series of research papers, our primary objective is to develop a set of precise numerical methods for solving the equations derived from the functional renormalization group in fluid dynamics, particularly focusing on the FRG flow equations. To establish this, we first review renormalization group theory and then delve into the fundamentals of the FRG, its applications in physics, and relevant concepts. Next, we investigate the parametric space for zero-dimensional quantum field theories, exploring how the FRG captures the behavior of these theories and the role of symmetry in the renormalization group flow. Our testing framework is then used to assess the accuracy of our numerical methods for solving the FRG flow equations in both symmetric and asymmetric cases, taking into account various perturbations of the theory. Finally, we provide an overview of our computational strategy and the results obtained, which demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach for investigating the properties of zero-dimensional quantum field theories.

The vast majority of music search platforms primarily rely on text-based queries to locate desired songs. While this approach proves effective for common song titles and artist names, it falls short when searching for less popular tracks or those with complex query patterns. For instance, users may struggle to find songs that match a specific genre, featuring a particular instrument, or conforming to a certain tempo. To bridge this gap, we introduce the concept of a meta query that enables users to refine their search within the music database by incorporating additional information beyond basic text descriptions. By integrating this feature into popular music platforms, we believe it has the potential to significantly enhance user experience and expand access to music content. To illustrate the potential of this idea, we present a basic implementation of a Pied Piper system, which we envision as a standalone music search platform that allows users to perform advanced searches based on various attributes of music.

This work formulates a theory of geometric configurations based on Lie groupoids and smooth stacks, establishing key connections to the theory of differential geometry. By leveraging the equivalence between smooth functors and sheaves of Lie groupoids, the concept of geometric configuration is generalized across categories using the framework of functorial geometry. Our research specifically explores configurations within a single category and focuses particularly on the functorial geometry of a single object. Furthermore, our findings are reinforced by connections to established theories of differential geometry.

Observations of molecular line emission reveal a large and rapidly rotating gas core at the center of the Dragon infrared dark cloud, suggesting it may be on the path to forming a high-mass star. Modeling this process involves analyzing the physical properties of the core and surrounding envelope, as well as the effects of non-local thermodynamic equilibrium transcriptions. By comparing models to observational data, we identify key differences and identify possible explanations, including the need for grain growth that warms the core's center and a potential collision between the core and an adjacent infrared dark cloud that is causing it to spin out of control.

This research paper formalizes the semantics of Godel's modal logic and its variations, including classical, intuitionistic, and positive propositional modal theories, within the context of relational structures and algebraic frameworks like Boolean algebra and Kleene algebra. The study establishes the equivalences between these abstract frameworks and various concrete structures, such as topological spaces, plant behavior specifications, and digital circuit designs. Building on this foundation, the paper introduces new algebraic and relational structures to represent reasoning patterns for prepositional modal logics, including Sahlqvist's 25 applicable languages, and subsequently proves the universality of these structures for their respective logics.

LiDAR technology is widely utilized for gathering detailed point cloud data across various settings, including construction, and to accommodate growing security requirements, the collection of data is frequently performed around the clock. While numerous advanced methods have been developed to automate processing of such data, especially for detecting and blocking hazards on roads, many existing techniques are primarily designed for use on systems from the same manufacturer. A unique approach has been presented that leverages deep learning to extract relevant information from LiDAR point clouds, enabling the detection of obstacles across multiple domains without the need for explicit scanning. In addition, this approach enables continuous data collection without posing additional workload on surveyors. A key innovation of this method is the development of a novel 3D metric learning framework that enables direct comparison of LiDAR point clouds. To validate this approach, it was tested on three diverse datasets in outdoor settings, and the results show its effectiveness and efficiency. The code and models for this project have been made publicly accessible.

The concept of one-step relations has been successfully applied to linear time-series models, and our research extends this concept to stationary stochastic processes on the sphere by defining one-step relations on the sphere. We establish statistically independent processes and derive conditions for the uniqueness of one-step relations. Our findings also enable the representation of a process's autocovariance operator in terms of its one-step relations. If you have access to the one-step relations at a given time point, this can be used to predict the process's mean and autocovariance operator at that time point. We discuss parameter estimation for one-step relations and demonstrate their applicability in modeling global atmospheric geopotential height data. Our research provides a new approach for modeling stationary stochastic processes and paves the way for exploring non-stationary processes on the sphere.

The source of ultra-high-energy cosmic particles, remaining a mystery for many decades, is a long-standing enigma in astrophysics, with numerous potential candidates and few clues on their origins. For the first time, researchers utilized eight years of data from the Fluorescence Detector and Muon Detector of the Telescope Array in the USA to look for neutrinos, which could be linked to cosmic rays and provide a possible route to understanding their source. Although no direct connections between neutrinos and cosmic rays were found, a unique approach revealed that excessive high-energy cosmic rays emanating from specific directions may be associated with neutrinos at a $3\sigma$ confidence level, which could be a first indication of finding the long-sought explanation for these cosmic phenomena.

The flow of a liquid foam is heavily influenced by two opposing phenomena: the benefits of shearing thick, syrup-like layers of gas bubbles and the hindrances posed by their breakdown. While both effects are significant, research indicates that the impact of shear should be minimized, particularly in highly viscous foams, to focus on the obstacles presented by the rough interfaces between bubbles. These obstacles take the form of grain boundary resistance, a concept supported by the results of experiments using a combination of glass and stainless steel as the material for the bubble walls. The shape of the resistance spectrum, however, remains unclear and requires further investigation. Some possible explanations include the presence of localized breakdowns and the interaction between neighboring bubbles, as well as the possibility of a more complex dependence on shear. The possibility of modifying the foam's properties to focus on shear cannot be ruled out either. Ultimately, the possibility of breaking down a highly viscous foam could depend on the balance between shear and point breakdowns of the bubble walls.

The detection of skin carcinomas, particularly in an unsupervised and unsegmented skin image context, is a complex task due to the presence of diverse skin disorders, artificial imperfections, and extraneous elements that hinder accurate identification. Current approaches primarily focus on supervised methods using deep learning for classification, yet they overlook the inherent disorder in the data that may indicate classification outliers. In contrast, our proposed framework combines a deep learning architecture with a novel anomaly detection component to simultaneously identify skin carcinomas and pinpoint data outliers in an unsupervised manner. Withstands external disturbances and artificial alterations in the training dataset that may mislead the network. The proposed framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through a comprehensive evaluation on the HSIS dataset, and the corresponding code and model are made available for public access.

The theory of finger growth in a Hele-Shaw cell is often used to model viscous finger formation in various situations. However, research has shown that certain factors can cause a deviation from the predicted pinching of the finger. While some of these factors lead to a curved finger shape, others result in a non-compact finger. Some possible explanations include the presence of surface tension, a rotating plate, or differences in fluid density. In this study, we investigate how these factors influence finger growth in a Hele-Shaw cell with a significant impact, particularly when the imposed stress is irregular. Our findings indicate that both surface tension and the factors affecting stress distribution can lead to a curved finger shape. Additionally, we have identified a stress discontinuity as the cause of non-compact finger behavior. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that normal-mode analysis can be used to explain the behavior of the Hele-Shaw cell when the imposed stress is regular.

In 1930, Vladimir Fock developed an innovative variational approach for describing classical dynamics. This method involves utilizing the Hamiltonian as a generating function to derive equations of motion, which can be expressed in a symmetric form that respects the structure of phase space. However, the main constraint of this method is that it maintains constant phase space volume, similar to Liouville's theorem. To overcome this limitation, we have developed a new strategy that leverages the concept of hamiltonian trajectories and expands the system in such a way that the initial conditions are met. This method enables the exploration of possible situations where the phase space volume is altered.

The presence of two distinct ethynyl cyclopentadiene (CHCCH) isomers has been identified in TMC-1, a dark cloud, by analyzing radio astronomy data from the Effelsberg 100m telescope using a single-dish radio telescope. This detection was made possible by employing a high signal-to-noise ratio and a high spectral resolution in the 8-9 GHz frequency range. By calculating the abundance of the two isomers and comparing it to a model of gas-grain chemical reactions, it was found that the abundance of the 1,2-ethynyl cyclopentadiene is significantly higher than the 1,3-ethynyl cyclopentadiene, at a ratio of approximately 5.5±1.5. This difference in abundance may be attributed to the varying reactivity of the two isomers in a molecular cloud environment.

In our proposed approach, we enhance neural machine translation using a look-ahead focus for creation that simulates human attention. This attention mechanism is grounded in human cognition, where attention is driven by intent and is often focused on achieving a specific goal related to the overall task. We have found that a particular sub-goal, which we call a "creation goal," is critical in understanding why a particular element of the input sentence is targeted. Our approach involves training two separate neural networks to share encoded representations of the input sentence. These networks have distinct "creation goals" that they strive to achieve, which influences their respective attention on the input sentence. We have demonstrated through experiments that our proposed approach transcends existing state-of-the-art methods in neural machine translation and also excel in other tasks that involve focused creation, such as summarization.

The advent of cloud computing has redefined how infrastructure and services are delivered, yet despite advancements, the fundamental principles of computer science remain underrepresented in university curriculum guidelines. To address this imbalance, a proven approach suggests utilizing real-world applications to teach computational concepts through a process known as translational methods. We share our experience adapting a well-established workshop on grid computing to teach computational paradigms to undergraduate students, highlighting how translating the framework into a cloud setting enhanced its effectiveness. Our goal is to encourage educators across various domains to adopt and build upon this approach, using our case study as a model for integrating practical technology behind computational concepts within curriculum guidelines.

A new cosmological model is presented which combines features of dark energy and dark matter through an adiabatic modification of gravity, requiring a negative pressure substance to maintain stability and consistency with the first law of thermodynamics. By applying a constant equation of state for this substance, the model's behavior is determined and its properties evaluated through various statistical tests, finding a good fit to the available cosmological data, including Hubble's constant and cosmic expansion rates.

Adopting an interpretive research approach, our study integrated physiological sensors and video recordings to explore the learning dynamics of a novel approach to curiosity called DPC (Curiosity with Different Intensities). Previous studies have established the importance of curiosity in the learning process. However, a lack of clear definitions and effective measurement tools has hindered progress. Our research fills this gap by introducing a unidimensional scale to measure curiosity and presenting a conceptual framework for studying learning dynamics through curiosity. This study was conducted in partnership with the Ontario Ministry of Education. Two experiments were performed to examine the efficacy of the PC-DPC approach in comparison to the traditional DPC method. The results showed that the PC-DPC approach yielded better outcomes, as evidenced by increased curiosity levels, a more diverse range of curiosity experiences, and improved learning outcomes. Furthermore, this study provides a theoretical framework for understanding how different curiosity intensities may shape each other and learning outcomes through various mechanisms.

Sparse representations form the basis for numerous machine learning methods, including neural networks, compression techniques, and regularization-based parameter estimation. One widely adopted approach involves enforcing an L1 norm constraint, resulting in a non-differentiable problem. To circumvent this issue, Gaussian processes are often used, which inherently incorporate smoothness through a particular kernel and face a less stringent sparsity-inducing prior. This paper focuses on developing a novel Gaussian process framework that leverages Mat\'ern kernels to enable sparse representations on structured domains, specifically graphs. By integrating a structured kernel that accounts for graph topology, the paper constructs a Gaussian process with a tractable posterior and derives an efficient optimization method that captures the target's underlying structure, ultimately leading to a data-driven graph generation application.

Metropolitan road discovery is an intriguing task that has been extensively explored using autonomous vehicles and sensor networks. This paper supplements existing research by illustrating the effectiveness of a system comprising a large number of ridesharing vehicles in optimizing road detection through a process called'system-level localization'. The underlying principle is that each vehicle, in an effort to minimize travel time between drop-off and pickup points, seeks to locate nearby roads, ultimately leading to a collective effort where multiple vehicles contribute to a shared map of local infrastructure. This process is both cooperative and competitive in nature. To model this, the paper presents a collaborative localization approach where the goal is to minimize time spent navigating between fixed points, incorporating potential changes in vehicle routes and the fact that detection of roads is subject to a sensor's limited field of view. This problem is then reformulated into an optimal discrete parallel task assignment problem. In order to illustrate the system's performance, a simulation is conducted using a a variety of vehicle configurations. The results show that even a relatively small number of vehicles can efficiently map major roads, and that the system's performance is largely dictated by the number of vehicles rather than their individual speed and sensing capabilities. Furthermore, the simulation reveals that even when routes are changed, previously mapped roads can be accurately localized, and that the system exhibits significant potential for future expansion and development.

A deviation in the decay rate of a J/psi particle into a single photon and an invisible pair of electrons could exceed the predicted margin by as much as 3.5 sigma if the necessary conditions are met. This discrepancy could be attributed to a combination of the J/psi decay into a single photon and an invisible pair of muons as well as the latter's decay into a single electron and a large amount of missing energy. If this deviation holds true, it would imply that a very small amount of muon mass exists, thus making it possible to reconcile the J/psi anomaly with a number of other anomalies through the application of a muon-based anomaly that extends beyond the lepton sector. As a result of this finding, it becomes necessary to incorporate a non-zero muon mass directly into a number of effective field theories that are related to neutrino and involve a non-minimal extension of the Higgs sector. This, in turn, could provide these theories with a more stable and consistent framework that is in line with the requirements of the dark energy phenomenon.

The basic structure of the explicit Strongly Stable Semi-implicit Dynamical System
Integration Method (SDIMSIM) has been generalized to accommodate variable timesteps.
This new approach maintains strong stability and accuracy of order two, making it suitable
for solving stiff problems. The method's performance is comparable to other implicit
Runge-Kutta methods, despite requiring less computational effort. A significant advantage
is derived from the minimal number of intermediate solutions needed during a step
calculation. A numerical example demonstrates the method's efficacy.

This study introduces the multivariate functional singular spectrum evaluation (MFSE) approach, enabling assessment of the dependence structure for multiple functions, specifically in scenarios involving one or more stationary time series, memory-based processes, and functional time series. Our research compares MFSE to established methods, including the functional version of the multivariate singular spectrum analysis (FMSSA), functional canonical analysis (FCOA), and applications of canonical correlation analysis (CCA), across various dimensional domains. As a result, MFSE emerges as a robust and effective method for evaluating the structural integrity of multivariate functional time series, outperforming competing methods in multiple scenarios.

The perceived reliability of human judgments in ranking importance is the basis of the AES framework, widely adopted in research and practice to guide theory testing and building. Nonetheless, numerous studies have shown that human subjectivity significantly distorts the validity of findings based on these judgments. The core issue lies in the inherent volatility of human preferences, which varies unpredictably with the slightest changes in experimental design or settings. Consequently, it is impractical to interpret results based on human rankings or judgments. In light of this, it is crucial to adopt alternative methodologies that minimize reliance on human subjectivity, such as using machine learning algorithms to reduce research costs and increase generalizability.

This research paper examines the long-term behavior of a random walker's persistence on a one-dimensional grid, specifically focusing on the time spent walking in the same direction. The study introduces a new approach to studying persistent random walk based on the concept of a local duration that is independent of the paradigm used (e.g., simple, random, biased). The paper shows that under certain conditions, the global persistence of a one-dimensional stochastic walk is equal to the average local duration. However, there are instances where the global persistence does not depend on the local duration, which is evident in a random walk with no persistence. The paper also compares its findings with existing research on persistent random walks.

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate key aspects of plasma-edge interactions under ITER-like conditions. IShTAR features a large, 12-meter long, tongue-shaped plasma chamber with an area of 1.2 square meters where a high-density plasma is created by an 80 kW helicon plasma generator operating in the 13.56 MHz frequency range. Due to the limited accessibility of the plasma inside the chamber, remote diagnosis of the plasma is essential for maintaining optimal generator performance and ensuring reliable operation. This contribution focuses on the spectroscopic analysis of the helicon-generated plasma using a sophisticated diagnostic system that incorporates multiple plasma diagnostics, including a Langmuir probe, an energy analyzer, a Thomson spectrometer, and an echellette spectrometer. By examining plasma parameters such as density, electron temperature, and flow velocity, the study confirms that the helicon generator produces a steady and consistent plasma state in the helicon mode of operation.

The significant rise in antibiotic resistance among plant-pathogenic bacteria necessitates innovative solutions, including microbial pesticides based on genetically modified strains of phytopathogenic nematodes. To effectively assess the efficacy of these pesticides, a modeling framework is presented, focusing on the population dynamics of the nematodes and their target plant-parasitic species. The framework models the population growth of the nematodes, taking into account birth, death, and reproductive rates, as well as the impact of environmental constraints and the presence of a bacterium that induces sterility. A numerical solution is implemented using a Runge-Kutta method, and a graphical user interface is provided for user input and results visualization. Simulations are presented to illustrate the application of the modeling framework, and future developments are proposed to incorporate additional aspects, such as host-pest interactions and the movement of nematodes within the soil.

This study presents a novel approach, W-Net, for automatically identifying and precisely outlining cell nuclei in histopathological images. These types of images contain rich spatial information about disease progression, allowing for accurate diagnosis through various analysis techniques such as tumor extent mapping and genetic mutation detection. However, analyzing such images manually is a time-consuming and error-prone process. To address this challenge, W-Net has been developed, leveraging advanced deep learning technology to efficiently and precisely extract essential information from these images. By testing W-Net on two widely used datasets, we have demonstrated its superior performance and user-friendly interface that enables users to fine-tune the system with ease. By incorporating optional user corrections, the system can be trained using only a small batch of annotated images, making it an ideal solution for a wide range of applications and providing a high level of user flexibility.

The converse Galois theory develops relationships between central simple algebras and their embedding fields, which are often tied to the properties of groups associated with those algebras. Given a central simple algebra defined over a field that is an extension of another field, the group in question is a subgroup of the group defined by the extension field, with the same order as the group defined by the original field. The Regional Converse Theorem establishes that if a central simple algebra is defined over a differential field that is a differential extension of another differential field, and if the algebraic group associated with the field is the same as an abelian division algebra-defined group, which includes symplectic and odd special orthogonal groups, then the differential field is a differential extension of another differential field. This theorem can be applied to show that if a central simple algebra-defined group, which includes even special orthogonal groups in a specific range, is an algebraic group associated with a differential field that is a differential extension of another differential field, then the differential field is a differential extension of another differential field.

A graph G is considered detectable if it possesses either a Hamiltonian cycle or an (n-1)-regular hamiltonian path, where n represents the number of vertices in G. This paper examines the properties of graphs that have been subjected to multiple iterations of line graphing and determines specific criteria that ensure these graphs remain detectable. Additionally, this paper introduces the concept of hamiltonian pathway index (hpi) to characterize the detectable nature of line graphs that have undergone repeated iterations. In particular, hpi is used to demonstrate that line graphs produced by an infinite number of iterations will eventually fail to detect certain hamiltonian patterns.

This research develops a one-dimensional cell model that captures the physiological, pathological, and treatment effects of pyroptosis induced by SARS-CoV-2. The model is derived from a comprehensive system of differential equations representing key cellular processes including metabolism, growth, and the initiation and execution of pyroptosis. The model's analysis focuses on a simplified version of the differential equations, revealing several critical dynamics that occur within the context of pyroptosis. These dynamics include the existence of a coexistence state between the cell and virus, as well as distinct periodic and aperiodic patterns of inflammation. The study also examines the efficacy of anti-inflammatory treatments in delaying cell death and virus replication.

External state variables and reinforcement learning methods can be used by self-interested agents to manipulate the learning process and distort the desired outcome. Recent research developed the concept of nearly optimal agent-independent reinforcement learning and implemented it through the RL99 framework, which assumes that an uninformed learner can achieve a nearly optimal solution after a certain number of trials. Building upon this work, we introduce a more stringent condition, RL99-strong, which demands that a strong, unbiased solution be attained with a certain probability after a certain number of trials. We prove that any learning process conforming to this condition can be free from manipulation by self-interested agents. Moreover, we outline a suitable technique for testing the strong, unbiased condition and an approach to adapt the condition to work with action spaces of any size. We also explore ways to eliminate state variables in deep reinforcement learning methods through the application of the condition to policy gradient methods and by incorporating the RL99-strong condition into the baseline-free objective, which yields an unmanipulable solution with a certain probability.

A blockchain-based smart contract on Tezos, dubbed a smart contract, is validated on the network through a proof-of-stake process that relies on the contributions of bakers who verify and vote on contracts before they are deployed. Given the importance of a thorough examination prior to voting, bakers need efficient and reliable methods to assess contracts accurately. To address this requirement, we present HELMHOLTZ, a cutting-edge validation tool developed specifically for Tezos contracts, leveraging the refinements module of the Coq proof assistant to ensure the accuracy and safety of contracts before they are deployed to the Tezos network. By integrating refinements with the Idris programming language, we demonstrate the feasibility of complex contract validation, and to showcase its capabilities, we provide a practical example of a validated contract from a real-world application.

In recent years, graph convolutional neural networks (GCNNs) have gained significant popularity due to their ability to effectively operate on graph-structured data without the need for extensive node feature extraction. Notwithstanding this success, numerous researchers have raised concerns regarding the non-trivial interpretation of the learned representations by GCNNs. In an effort to address this issue, a novel framework has been proposed that matches the filtering process in GCNNs to the frequency response spectrum of a neural network, thereby providing a detailed analysis of the spectral characteristics that GCNNs can learn. Furthermore, our framework is versatile and can be applied to a wide range of neural networks working with frequency-based data structures. In the context of GCNNs, our results indicate that these networks are capable of learning spatial frequency responses from local neighborhood aggregates and spectral frequency responses from a global diffusion process. Building upon this understanding, a new model has been proposed that integrates both local and global frequency responses within a neural network, and through thorough experiments and evaluations, our proposed model has demonstrated superior performance compared to existing GCNNs.

By modifying the Chern-Simons action with the addition of a scalar field, it's possible to derive a gravity system that includes a source term. This modification yields a consistent and well-defined theory for gravity within the context of the theory, allowing for solutions to the gravitational field equations to be determined through a gauge transformation. The relationship between the gravitational field and the scalar field can be described using a hydrodynamical analogy, where the properties of spinning hairy black holes and solitons, including their temperatures and chemical potentials, are depicted graphically using a set of self-similar curves. The influence of a non-zero cosmological constant can also be shown to result in the merging of two solitons into a single spinning soliton. The ability to depict these solutions graphically relies on the absence of a stable non-rotating soliton solution. The paper also explores the relationship between the added source term and the cosmological constant, demonstrating how it can give rise to solutions with non-zero chemical potential and temperature. The existence of solutions with chemical potential cannot be accommodated within an asymptotically anti-de Sitter spacetime. The paper goes on to consider solutions with a non-zero source term in topologically trivial and non-trivial spacetimes. In the case of a non-trivial spacetime, solutions with non-zero chemical potential and temperature become possible. The paper also examines solutions within an Einstein gravity context, showing how they can be derived from an SU(2) Chern-Simons

We've observed a novel phenomenon in systems with reversible symmetries, where the thermal equilibrium configurations are isotropic and display Bragg-like blurring. This peculiar behavior is unique to systems with reversible symotries, and we've found that any irreversible symmetry disrupts this phenomenon, leading to anisotropic thermal equilibria that exhibit crystal-like patterns. This discovery implies that certain non-reversible transformations can induce a shift from bragg-like blurring to crystal-like patterns, and we've demonstrated this by applying a specific non-reversible transformation to a system with reversible symmetries - the motion of a brane within that system.

This paper presents a novel approach to enhance the accuracy of ultrasound elastography by correcting lateral displacement measurements. The traditional virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) method is modified to reduce errors in estimation, and a new algorithm is developed to minimize the noise effect on the corrected measurements. In vitro experiments using a phantom and simulations verify the improved performance of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the new VSSA method is more effective than conventional elastography techniques in noise-free conditions and outperforms the standard VSSA method in the presence of noise.

Students learn programming best through hands-on coding, but they also need to understand algorithms and flow of programs. To bridge this gap, a secondary benefit is achieved - preparing students for success in careers where automated tools are used. However, writing code is not the only way for students to understand algorithms; a new method is proposed that allows algorithms to be explained using pseudocode containing variables of different types and control structures. This approach is shown to be effective by presenting an online platform and a related educational approach that's being tested in a classroom setting.

The boolean function $\mathrm{Bt}$ generates a family of boolean posets that maintain a consistent pattern of minimality, thereby ensuring that any subset of size $r$ contains an element inferior to all members of a corresponding subset of size $r$. This principle is applied to demonstrate the consistency of a poset related to boolean structures, as well as to establish the existence of a particular set of numbers that satisfies the conditions of a more general theory.

In the context of information retrieval, where we have a dataset of $n$ points in $d$ dimensions and a target parameter $k$, a significant challenge lies in identifying a subset of $k$ centers that can effectively group the remaining data efficiently. The standard $k$-means clustering algorithm achieves optimal results but suffers from a substantial computational cost, making it impractical for large-scale data sets. In contrast, a range of dynamic algorithms has been developed to strike a balance between performance and efficiency, with most existing analyses focusing on results in lower-dimensional spaces or with specific structural characteristics. In this paper, we introduce a new, simple and efficient dynamic $k$-means algorithm based on random sampling, which produces a center subset that can group the data in $O(nt)$ time, with a significant reduction in computational cost compared to traditional methods. We establish a non-uniform upper bound on the covering ratio of the data with a factor of $O(k^{3/2})$, which is close to the best known lower bound for at least two times the target size. This upper bound applies to any data set with a unique structure and holds a general form, with a value of $O(k^{3/2})$ covering the special cases of data sets with specific structures. Building upon this result, we demonstrate an almost optimal dynamic $k$-means algorithm with a cover ratio of $O(k^{3/2})$ for general data sets, with a time complexity of

We introduce hierarchical models of cooperation that integrate the core elements of reinforcement learning and strategic interaction, developing a framework that captures both individual decisions and collective actions in a comprehensive manner. Specifically, we establish a framework for cooperative behavior that addresses a broad category of cooperative problems, and then focus on a significant subclass by defining cooperative PWDL games as those where cooperation yields a safer escape from a bounded territory than individual action. We establish theoretical conditions for a wide range of PWDL games that involve near-optimal cooperative solutions, and we verify these principles through a series of computer simulations. Our study provides a foundational framework for examining the intricate dynamics of cooperative behavior in complex social settings.

A nontransitive likelihood outcome among three alternatives can lead to circular reasoning. This concept is often associated with the work of Barnard (1972) and has been applied to develop a permutational symmetry in statistical testing. Barnard's condition for a likelihood nontransitivity has been conditionally met by all tested datasets from 1880 to 2016. These results suggest that nontransitive likelihoods are an inherent feature of real data sets, making the usual practice of selecting the most likely option questionable. Furthermore, a new condition has been proposed to guarantee a nontransitive likelihood in a circular fashion. This new condition is met by a well-known dataset from 1991. Both conditions can be seen as two different interpretations of Barnard's condition.

Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their superior performance over traditional image processing methods. A popular approach known as unsupervised learning using CycleGAN has been widely adopted for enhancing high-dose CT images based on low-dose CT images, with several variations being proposed to incorporate adversarial and cycle consistency loss functions. However, most existing methods fail to utilize the adversarial training process effectively, as they do not consider the adversarial domain classification loss as an auxiliary loss. Another limitation is that the cycle consistency loss is applied directly to the image inputs, which can lead to over-smoothing of noise in low-dose CT images. To address these issues, we propose modifying the CycleGAN framework in an adaptive instance normalization switchable cycle, by treating the adversarial domain classification as a primary task and introducing a cycle consistency loss for the noise reduction in high-dose CT images only. The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance in PSNR and SSIM metrics, as evaluated on a publicly available dataset of abdominal CT images.

Despite significant advancements in dialog comprehension tasks through pre-trained models, there's still a notable performance gap when compared to other comprehension tasks like reading comprehension. To bridge this disparity, our proposal incorporates semi-supervised contrasting to pre-train conversational language models to emphasize the comprehension component in dialog tasks. Unlike prior methods that used paired data for contrasting, we suggest using tree-structured contrasting to leverage the rich syntactic and semantic structure inherent in dialogs. Through evaluation on the SICK-Newset dataset and the Dialog BERT dataset, our pre-trained models exhibit enhanced performance, showcasing the effectiveness of semi-supervised contrasting in pre-training for dialog comprehension.

This research aims to establish a relationship between the conformal Ricci-Yamabe soliton, a specific variant of the Ricci-Yamabe soliton, and an ideal fluid spacetime with a particular compatibility condition. By demonstrating that a conformal Ricci-Yamabe soliton is equivalent to an ideal fluid spacetime with a compatible Ricci-Yamabe flow, the research provides an link between these two concepts. A key aspect of this relationship is the identification of a compatible tensor field, which arises from the condition of the ideal fluid spacetime. This connection between the soliton and the fluid spacetime establishes a geometric framework that can be used to derive a theorem related to the conformal Ricci-Yamabe soliton.

To study the rotational characteristics of distorted halo nuclei, we employed the deformed relativistic Hartree-Slater procedure in its self-consistent form. By investigating the rotational patterns of $^{32}$Mg, $^{40}$Magnesium, and $^{42}$Magnesium, which possess large neutron shells and exhibit halo distortions, we found that the deformed $1^+$ excitations are not always straightforwardly related to the expected rotational $2^+$ state and may instead follow a more complex pattern due to decoupling effects.

Video super-resolution is the process of enhancing video frames that are downgraded, either naturally (due to blurry video from the past) or artificially (video compression). Despite the importance of this task, video super-resolution remains a challenging task for computer vision because it involves reconstructing detailed frames based on grainy input images. Previous attempts have been made to solve this problem using recurrent and transformer-based models, but their success was limited by several factors, including the slow transmission of visual information between frames and the misalignment of feature maps. To build upon these attempts, our research introduces the BasicVSR++ model, which improves video super-resolution by introducing a more effective and efficient way to transmit and align frame features. By incorporating a lightweight and bidirectional telepathy connection, our model is able to learn and apply more precise and consistent transformation information across frames, resulting in state-of-the-art performance on the Vid4 dataset and competitive performance on the UrbanFlow dataset, even without optimization techniques commonly used in video super-resolution.

Precise vector boson reconstruction is crucial for the analysis of high-energy muon interactions, particularly in experiments like the LHCb forward spectrometer where long muon trajectories allow for pulse shape analysis. The efficient estimation of a weak boson's momentum, often required in these analyses, is inherently linked to the accuracy of the muon's momentum and the energy of the incoming photon. Consequently, reconstructing the boson efficiently necessitates a thorough understanding of muon and photon interactions. This paper will outline the development of a highly efficient photon flux estimator, a novel dispersion relation for muons in the form of a scalar product with the energy-momentum tensor, and the associated corrections for the energy and muon momentum. These advancements will be integrated into a revised estimator for the efficient calculation of vector boson momentum.

In complex reinforcement learning systems with multiple tasks, where shared components play a crucial role, the usual practice of isolating learning dynamics fails to produce desired results. This is because subsystems and system as a whole exhibit interconnected dynamics, leading to uncontrolled fluctuations, catastrophic interference, and slow recovery from setbacks. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principles of modern control systems and propose the concept of a variable adaptive critic to decouple learning by separating the mapping between desired performance and actual behavior. This allows for the optimization of a critical subsystem that maps desired performance to actual behavior, making it possible to leverage a method known as extended series expansion to enhance adaptability. This approach is mathematically equivalent to an efficient way to learn by generating an infinite number of approximate models through cumulative experiences. We integrate our framework with a progressive multi-task learning paradigm that facilitates seamless transition between tasks by minimizing the necessity for readaptation. As a result, we achieve a significant improvement (up to 3.5 times) in performance and a substantial reduction (by more than 5 times) in the number of training iterations required in comparison to state-of-the-art models.

In this research, we establish precise approximations of the solution to time fractional porous medium equation and time fractional Swift-Hohenberg equation on a noncompact open set with varying coefficients. The novel technique employs the Bony-Laplace method and the Baker-Chui-Wang representation of functions. We also extend our findings to a subclass of time fractional Allen-Cahn equation using the superposition principle.

Kurt Godel, along with colleagues Alonzo Church, Stephen Kleene, and Rosser, first discussed the concept of a universal theorem in 1930. Not long after, Godel, in his famous 1930 lecture, referred to the potential for a universal theorem to be used in a diagonalization argument. In 1931, Godel published his famous incompleteness theorems, and the following year Church proved the existence of a universal theorem. In the early 1930s, Kleene and Rosser developed methods for constructing models that avoided the possibility of a universal true sentence existing, achieving this by essentially 'killing' any universal sentence through their construction.
